articles.title: Abbott spent 12 years neglecting Texas air pollution – a new governor can start cleaning it up
articles.author: Daniel Cohan, Professor of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Rice University
paras: When air quality monitors in 10 Texas counties showed soot above the new federal health limit in 2024, Gov. Greg Abbott faced a choice. He could direct the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to develop plans to cut air pollution in all 10. Or he could heed the agency’s advice: blame six counties’ pollution mostly on sources beyond Texas, and clean up just four.

Abbott chose neither. Weeks after President Donald Trump returned to office in 2025, the governor asked the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to declare the entire state in compliance with the federal standard for fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5. If the EPA agreed, Texas would skirt the need to write a plan to control the deadliest air pollutant.

As an atmospheric scientist, I was stunned. I had seen Texas and other states do too little to control air pollution for years. But I hadn’t imagined a governor would override his own regulators to avoid making a plan altogether.
Texas air pollution had declined for decades, but during Abbott’s 12 years in office, progress in reducing PM2.5 and ozone smog largely stalled.
Now, the election of Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa to succeed Abbott in January 2027 offers a chance to get Texas pollution trending downward again.

Hinojosa has a history of supporting efforts to clean up pollution, including a climate plan proposed in 2021 to cut emissions. But progress won’t come easily. Abbott’s appointees still run the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, and Republicans still control the state Senate.

PM2.5 is tiny, with diameters of 2.5 microns or less, so it can be inhaled deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. Exposure has been linked to heart attacks, strokes, respiratory problems and many other ailments.

Some PM2.5 is emitted directly as particles, such as in diesel exhaust and wildfire smoke. Other particles form in the atmosphere from sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbon gases emitted by power plants, vehicles and other sources.
Abbott’s dodge of PM2.5 standards fit a pattern of going easy on polluters.

Houston and Dallas have missed deadline after deadline to meet federal ozone standards. State regulators blame much of the smog on foreign sources. This fall, Abbott persuaded the Trump administration to reconsider how severely the two regions’ smog is classified, a step that could loosen the pollution controls required there.

Under Abbott, state regulators have also rarely cracked down on unauthorized pollution releases. Of 21,769 such events reported by refineries, chemical plants and other facilities over six years, they classified fewer than 1% as “excessive,” the designation that requires a company to fix the problem.

Texas’ coal power plants emit more sulfur dioxide than any other state’s. That gas forms sulfate particles, a major ingredient of PM2.5 and haze. Federal rules have required new coal plants to install scrubbers, which remove sulfur dioxide from smokestack gases, since 1979. But older plants were exempted, and several in Texas still run without them.

A 2016 Obama administration plan to reduce Texas’ haze and a narrower Biden administration proposal in 2023 would have required several plants to install or upgrade scrubbers. In 2025 the Trump administration accepted Texas’ own haze plans, which required no new scrubbers. Critics of the federal plans had warned that some plants would close instead because of the cost, reducing electricity supplies.

But scrubbers are a long-established technology, and their health benefits dwarf their costs. When I worked at Georgia’s environmental agency in the mid-2000s, we negotiated a timetable for Georgia Power to install scrubbers and retire outdated plants. Atlanta’s PM2.5 levels fell about 40% over the next decade, and the lights stayed on just fine.

Research by my group at Rice University has found that PM2.5 from Texas coal plants, formed mostly from their sulfur dioxide, kills hundreds of people a year. Wind and solar power or geothermal energy could replace their output, with batteries filling in when winds are slow and sunshine weak.
No polluter has benefited more from Abbott’s neglect than the W.A. Parish power plant, whose smokestacks loom over my hikes at Brazos Bend State Park southwest of Houston.

Three of its four coal units have no scrubbers at all. Parish emitted three times as much sulfur dioxide as all other facilities in the Houston region combined in 2024. Our modeling linked its pollution to 177 deaths a year. Since sulfate, which forms from sulfur dioxide, is the second-largest ingredient in Houston’s PM2.5, any serious cleanup plan would have to tackle Parish.
Hinojosa’s first test will come within weeks of her inauguration, when the U.S. EPA faces a court-ordered deadline to announce which counties violate its PM2.5 standard.

The number of Texas counties exceeding the limit is now at 14. Wildfire smoke and other exceptional events may explain some of the problem, but most of those counties need plans to cut the local emissions driving their PM2.5 levels.
Hinojosa can withdraw Abbott’s zero-county request and ask the EPA to designate counties as failing to meet the standard where the data warrants it, triggering a need to write cleanup plans.

In my view, those plans should start with overdue controls on emissions at the dirtiest coal plants. The state also needs to cut pollution from refineries, chemical plants, industrial flares and ports to meet the standards. Expanding grants to replace old diesel engines would cut soot and smog.

Better plans would include more monitors. Many counties, including Fort Bend, Texas’ eighth-most-populous county and home to Parish, don’t have a single PM2.5 monitor. Others don’t measure what their PM2.5 is made of. Because PM2.5 is a stew of carbon, sulfate, nitrate, ammonium, dust and other compounds, knowing the mix is key to controlling it cost-effectively.
Abbott spent 12 years explaining away Texas’ dirty air. A new governor can finally clear it.

articles.title: Lowering fuel-efficiency standards for cars could cost Americans more, not save them money
articles.author: Benjamin Paul Leard, Associate Professor of Economics, University of Tennessee
paras: When looking to purchase a car, many people hesitate to buy one that could reduce their fuel costs, even when gas prices are high. The Trump administration has made that decision more complex for consumers.

Cars with lower fuel costs tend to be more expensive to purchase, may be inconvenient to refuel or may have less trunk space. Conventional gasoline engine models often have lower up-front prices and standard features, including easy refueling and cargo space, which keeps consumers buying them.

Since taking office, the Trump administration has eliminated limits on greenhouse gas emissions from vehicles and rolled back future standards for vehicle fuel efficiency, allowing future passenger vehicles to consume more gas per mile traveled than what would have been allowed under existing rules. The administration claimed those actions would save people money.

Specifically, the administration said the fact that it’s cheaper to build less-efficient cars would mean consumers would pay prices so low that the savings would offset any additional costs for fuel over the life of the car.

However, the article we recently published in the journal Science explains that the administration’s decision is based on several flawed assumptions, including how much buyers care about their cars’ future fuel costs. We found that the administration’s regulation changes will leave U.S. car buyers worse off because they will spend far more on gas relative to the up-front price savings, especially if gasoline prices remain high for a long period.
An example of fuel efficiency savings

Take a look at two comparable cars: a gas-powered 2026 Toyota Corolla and a 2026 Toyota Corolla hybrid powered with a combination of gas and electricity. The base model hybrid costs $1,800 more to buy than the base model gas-powered car.

The gas car has an average fuel efficiency of 34 miles per gallon; the hybrid’s is 50 miles per gallon. To drive the same distance, the hybrid’s increased efficiency saves $550 a year in fuel costs, assuming gas costs $4 per gallon.

So after about three years and a few months, the gas savings of the Toyota hybrid will have evened out its higher purchase price. Some cars take longer to break even: The fuel savings from a Honda Accord hybrid will take about eight years. But the average car is nearly 13 years old – meaning fuel savings will continue for a decade after the owner has broken even on the higher sticker price.
Examining economic assumptions

In its analysis of the economic effects of the loosened restrictions, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency assumed that consumers sacrifice valuable vehicle features when buying a more fuel-efficient vehicle.

For instance, the agency pointed to people being annoyed by certain fuel-saving technologies such as stop-start ignition, which shuts off the engine at a red light in certain types of vehicles, or the difficulty of charging an electric vehicle away from home. It projected that people prefer cars without stop-start ignition and without the need to charge batteries.

Furthermore, the EPA assumed that gasoline prices would never exceed $3.50 per gallon, a level far lower than current average prices. While the EPA agreed that a less-fuel-efficient car would cost more to refuel, it also claimed that consumers would lose about 75% to 79% of those fuel cost savings because of unhappiness with certain fuel-saving technologies or the inconvenience of refueling electric vehicles.

However, after reviewing studies on how much people value different attributes of various vehicles, we found the evidence showed consumers would be willing to pay only 17% to 31% of those additional fuel costs.

Therefore, while consumers would pay a lower up-front purchase price if fuel-efficiency standards remained high, they would not find enough value in desirable features on the cars to make up for higher recurring spending on gasoline. And that does not even consider the environmental costs, including damage associated with greenhouse gas emissions, which is influencing U.S. car buyers’ choices.

In fact, given the recent improvement in features of EVs and charging infrastructure, we believe that the agencies may have overestimated those costs by even more. Many current new EVs have around 300 miles of range before needing to be recharged. That’s much farther than cars available even five years ago.
Messages to car manufacturers
Making matters more difficult for consumers is the fact that recent presidents have sent mixed messages to automakers.
The Obama administration set aggressive standards for improving fuel economy and reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

The first Trump administration rolled back those standards. The Biden administration not only reinstated the Obama standards but went beyond them, requiring further increases in fuel efficiency and emissions reductions.

The second Trump administration’s moves to reverse the Biden standards have left automakers unclear about how to develop long-term plans for what to build and sell. That planning happens years in advance.

In 2025, when Trump discontinued federal tax subsidies to help people buy electric cars, automakers stopped building as many. With the fuel-efficiency changes, many automakers have shifted away from introducing new EV models and toward promoting gasoline models.

Fewer electric cars makes it more challenging for people to buy them. In the U.S., according to September 2026 sales data, all-electric cars account for about 7% of new car sales – while in China, where electric cars abound and are subsidized by the government, around 40% of new cars people bought in 2026 were all-electric.

Our work finds that eliminating the greenhouse gas emissions standards and weakening the fuel-efficiency rules will bring Americans more pain at the pump and hurt people’s wallets, making living less affordable.
Benjamin Paul Leard is affiliated with the University of Tennessee and Resources for the Future.

articles.title: Switching devices off standby can save £45 a year – practical advice on energy bills from an expert
articles.author: Stuart Walker, Research Fellow in Sustainabilty Assessment, University of Sheffield
paras: As the weather turns colder and with energy bills predicted to rise, it’s the time of year when we look for ways to heat our homes more cost-effectively.

Gas and electricity bills for a typical UK home are predicted to rise by 26% from January. Some financial support is promised by the government, including the household energy payment of £100 to many households in England and a VAT cut on electricity bills until July. In most cases, though, these measures will not offset the increase in bills, which is projected to be around £443 for a typical household.

The UK has a high proportion of older properties, with 78% having been built before 1980. This means UK homes are often not as energy efficient as they could be, making them expensive to heat. Heat pumps, batteries, solar panels and full retrofit projects may ultimately reduce energy bills, but are expensive. Just 1.1% of homes in England and Wales reach an energy performance certificate score of A, and the vast majority (around 72%) score C or D, so there opportunities for all of us to improve our homes.

Draughts (cold air entering the house from outside, or entering a warm room from a colder one) dilute the warm air in the room with colder air, meaning our heating has to work harder to replace it. What’s more, draughts can make us feel cold even in a warm room, because air movement across our skin has a cooling effect.

The most common sources of draughts are windows, doors and letterboxes. Walking around your home on a cold or windy day will highlight any draughts. In many cases, draught-proofing can be a relatively cheap DIY job. Guidance from charity the Centre for Sustainable Energy explains how to go about it. A DIY draught excluder for the bottom of the door can be quite easy to make, and cut out some of the cold. A curtain behind the door is also effective, but make sure it’s wide enough to cover gaps around and below the door.

Energy advice charity the Energy Saving Trust suggests that professional window and door draught-proofing could save around £55 per year, and a chimney draught excluder could save another £45 per year.

If the heat in our homes escapes, our heating has to replace it, which uses energy and costs money. Insulation stops this happening. Our homes should be insulated on all sides. This means the floor, walls, and roof.

In homes with a loft, this is often the easiest place to insulate. Loft insulation helps reduce heat loss through the roof. Insulating a loft now will reduce bills for years to come. This can be a DIY job, or can be done by a professional. Organisations such as the National Insulation Association can help find an installer.

If your loft is already insulated, you can add more insulation. The current minimum recommendation for new properties is 270mm, and increasing yours from 120mm to this level could save around £17-£20 per year. If you currently have less insulation, the saving will be much greater.
If you have a hot water cylinder, it’s also worth checking its insulation and adding or improving it. Insulating an uninsulated cylinder could save £200.
In properties with single glazing, heat loss from windows will be large. While installing double glazing is a big job, long term benefits are large.

It is sometimes suggested that leaving your heating on at a low level can lead to lower total energy use than turning it on and off. Whether or not this is true depends on your house, your heating, and you.

A detached house with thick stone walls will take a long time to become warm, but will stay warm for longer (this is also true in summer, and is the reason churches and old buildings remain cool in summer). A newer house with brick and plasterboard walls will heat up more quickly, but also loses heat more quickly.

It’s often better to maintain temperature in the thick walled older house, so here it might be better to adopt the “low and slow” method, particularly if you have a heat pump or a modern boiler. If you have a newer house, turning the heating on and off is likely to be the cheaper option in the long run. Using a smart meter, it’s possible to test both options for a week or so, then adopt the best option.

Heating is a major contributor to energy use, but it’s not the only one. Cooking, lighting, hot water and appliances all play a part. If you have any old-fashioned light bulbs, swapping them for LEDs immediately can save around £45-£55 a year. Using lids on pans, only boiling the water you need, turning off your oven and letting food finish cooking in the leftover heat, and avoiding the tumble dryer wherever possible are all good ways to save energy and money.

There are many other practical options, such as reflecting film behind your radiators, to reduce your energy bills without too much hard work. Just switching devices off standby could save £45 annually. Then of course there’s also looking at changing your energy supplier or making the most of cheaper electricity overnight. We haven’t included every option here, but energy advice services such as the Energy Saving Trust and charity the Fuelbank foundation can all help.

If you’re considering a bigger project and want to really understand how your house loses heat and prepare yourself for the winter, there are charities and organisations across the UK who offer surveys, or may have infrared cameras available to borrow.

A survey will tell you where your house is losing heat so you can target your efforts in the right place. Some are available for free, and even if you’re not planning major work can provide useful information on cold spots and missing insulation. You could start with charity the National Energy Action.
Stuart Walker is affiliated with the Grantham Centre for Sustainable Futures, University of Sheffield, and Hope Valley Climate Action.

articles.title: Cop31: the world is heading for climate ‘overshoot’ – the UN summit must start planning for what comes next
articles.author: Michael Jacobs, Professor of Political Economy, University of Sheffield
paras: A surprising thing has happened at the UN climate conference, Cop31, as it gears up to its conclusion in Antalya, Turkey. Negotiators are discussing how to cool the planet.

You might think this should not be surprising, but how to respond to the latest climate science was not on the agenda when the meeting started. Now, the summit’s latest draft decision explicitly recognises a role for carbon dioxide removal (CDR) alongside deep emissions cuts. This is a significant shift, driven by pressure from some of the countries most vulnerable to climate change – the small island states – in response to two alarming scientific reports in the last month.

The World Meteorological Organization has confirmed that the rate at which the Earth is heating up is accelerating. One reason is the planet is becoming less “reflective”: the loss of ice and snow, changes in cloud formation and (paradoxically) reductions in atmospheric pollution means that more solar radiation is being absorbed rather than reflected into space.

The result is that the Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5°C will not be met. There’s a new term for this new warming trajectory: “overshoot”. As a United Nations Environment Programme (Unep) report explains, the best we can hope for now is to exceed 1.5°C but then limit the extent of the overshoot, peaking emissions as soon as possible and then returning to 1.5°C later in the century.

Unfortunately, Unep also notes that this may be easier said than done. The longer temperatures remain above 1.5°C, the greater the risk of triggering irreversible changes to systems such as polar ice sheets and glaciers, ocean currents and the Amazon rainforest, which could make returning to lower temperatures impossible.

Up until now we have thought there were basically two responses to global heating. We needed to cut emissions (mitigation), and cope with the warming we experienced (adaptation). But overshoot means that achieving net zero emissions is not enough. By the time we get there the temperature will be too high.

Overshoot will require two other kinds of response. As well as cutting the flow of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere, we can physically take them out, a process known as carbon dioxide removal or CDR.

And we will also need to consider different ways to increase the planet’s reflectivity. These include limiting aircraft contrails (which trap heat), expanding the white surface areas of the earth (both buildings and crops), or making glaciers more stable. It could potentially include various methods of “solar radiation management”, such as brightening clouds over the oceans, or injecting reflective aerosols into the stratosphere. If any of these “climate cooling” technologies could help bring temperatures down, they need much more carefully governed research.

Removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere is not the same as carbon capture and storage (CCS), which refers to the capture of emissions from industrial plants before they reach the atmosphere. In all net zero scenarios CCS is needed to deal with the residual emissions of fossil fuels. But we now know CDR is going to be required as well – first alongside emissions reduction, to slow warming down, and then to return the global temperature to a safer level.

There are various potential removal methods. Some are familiar and uncontroversial, though not yet being done at anything like the required scale. These are natural processes such as tree-planting, restoring ecosystems and improving carbon in soils.

Other “novel” forms of CDR are still in development. Carbon uptake methods in the oceans include enhancing the ocean’s alkalinity and the fertilisation of phytoplankton by adding iron. On land, enhanced natural processes include adding charcoal to soils (“biochar”), and accelerating the creation of carbonates from rock weathering.

There are also more technological interventions. These include “bioenergy with carbon capture and storage” (Beccs), in which biomass is burned for energy and the emissions captured and stored underground; and “direct air capture”, the removal of CO₂ from the air with advanced machines.

All of these methods are now being piloted, but remain expensive. Some of them also raise environmental risks: before any could be used at significant scale, countries would need to be sure that they would not have negative side-effects. In turn that means the world needs to think seriously about their governance.
The politics of cooling the planet

But there is currently no place for such talks. Neither novel methods of carbon dioxide removal, nor increasing the earth’s reflectivity, are formally part of the Cop negotiations or indeed any other UN policy process.

This is because many countries have believed that any discussion of these would take the pressure off emissions reduction. They have been supported in this view by some of the larger climate NGOs, who have not wanted anything to distract from their campaign against fossil fuels.

But the world has changed. Climate science says emissions reduction on its own can no longer keep us on a safe climate pathway. This surely makes blanket opposition to novel CDR and cooling methods untenable. Governments need to be scaling up research into these methods and considering their governance. At the very least, they should be talking about them.

This is why the latest moves at Cop31 are so important. At this point it is not clear whether countries will agree to a statement on how to respond to overshoot. Some are still opposed. But if the final text does acknowledge that active cooling will be needed, it will mark the beginning of a new era in climate action.

Michael Jacobs receives funding from the Climate Hub, a non-profit organisation aiming to raise awareness of the latest climate science and its implications for policy. He is a member of the Labour Party.

articles.title: Florida’s flooding déjà vu is a sign of things to come – so, who is most at risk and how can they prepare?
articles.author: Smitha Rao, Associate Professor of Social Work, The Ohio State University
paras: Floodwater filled the streets and crept into homes across Florida’s Atlantic coast as an intense storm dumped more than a foot of rain in 24 hours starting Nov. 17, 2026. The deluge followed extreme downpours in parts of the region less than three weeks earlier, and forecasters warned of more rain still to come.
As people in Fort Lauderdale watched the water rise in their already saturated yards, it may have felt like déjà vu.
In April 2023, more than 25 inches of rain fell in Fort Lauderdale in 24 hours. Even hurricanes rarely drop that much rain in one area that fast. Residents could do little to stop the flooding.
Studies show that as global temperatures rise, more people will be at risk from such destructive flooding – including in areas that rarely faced extreme flooding in the past.

In many of these communities, the people at greatest risk of harm from flash flooding are low-wage workers, older adults and other vulnerable residents who live in low-lying areas and who have few resources to protect their properties and themselves.

I study the impact of extreme weather on vulnerable communities as an associate professor of social work. To limit the damage, communities need to know who is at risk and how they can be better prepared.
More extreme downpours in a warming world
The Florida storms offer a view into the risks ahead as temperatures rise. These risks are especially high as the effects of a strong 2026-27 El Niño set in.

A warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, leading to stronger downpours. The resulting deluges can be devastating. These events are expected to increase in frequency and intensity in many regions as greenhouse gas emissions from human activities continue to heat up the planet.
Recent disasters show how the risk of flash flooding is expanding beyond areas traditionally considered at risk.
Knowing who is most at risk
To plan for extreme weather, it’s crucial for community leaders and residents to know where the risks are highest and who might not be prepared.

Low-lying areas with poorly planned development, lack of investment in protective infrastructure and the lingering effects of historic disinvestment and discrimination are often at higher risk. So are low-income communities with tight budgets that can’t afford protective measures like upgraded levees or stormwater systems and can’t recover from damage quickly.

When older adults live in these flood-prone areas, they are at even higher risk. Older adults have a higher likelihood of having health needs or some form of disability that could affect their ability to leave quickly during a disaster. They are also more likely to be socially isolated, which may mean they don’t hear timely information or have help to evacuate or quick access to resources for recovering.
Renters and the impact of housing insecurity

My colleagues and I have examined how prepared people are for disasters of any kind across the U.S. – flooding, tornadoes, hurricanes and others – and how housing security played a role. The numbers are sobering.

Overall, we found in a 2023 study that 57% of the population, among 29,070 housing units surveyed nationwide, reported they were not prepared with food, water, emergency funds and transportation in case disaster struck. We found that households facing housing insecurity – those behind on their payments for rent, mortgage or utilities – were less prepared for disasters than others, even when the occupants had similar incomes and education.

People who are struggling to meet day-to-day needs often don’t have the ability and resources to plan for everyday events, let alone for disasters. Our research has shown that households with children, households led by women, and low-income households were less prepared than others for disasters.

Renting adds additional challenges. In the U.S., lower-income families often depend on the rental market. They tend to move more frequently, and since they don’t own the property, they often can’t make upgrades for safety. And landlords might not prioritize those risks that seem rare but carry costs.
How to help communities stay safe
The most effective way to address these challenges is through solutions that are tailored to the community.

That can involve investing in infrastructure, including state-funded priorities such as drainage systems, large-scale flood prevention measures and strengthening the power grid, as well as ensuring that people have access to safe and affordable housing. Some communities and federal agencies have bought out properties that frequently flood and changed zoning rules to prevent more people from moving into harm’s way.
Raising community awareness about climate change and extreme weather risks is also crucial, especially among those most at risk, such as older adults and other socially marginalized groups.

If people understand the risks, know how to prepare their homes, know how to plan for emergencies, know whom to contact for help, and have stronger systems of care, they’re more likely to be prepared when disasters strike.
I believe the most successful efforts are those that bring at-risk communities into planning discussions.

For example, in Columbus, Ohio, the city partnered with the Central Ohio Area Agency on Aging, Age Friendly Innovation Center and my team to improve disaster preparedness among older residents. We worked with older adults in affordable housing communities and the human service professionals who support them to help design action plans for communities with special needs in the event of an emergency. The tool kit we created can help social service providers prepare low-income residents for extreme weather.

Our team is now working with service providers nationwide to document best practices, identify gaps and ensure residents are better prepared for climate- and weather-related emergencies in the future.
This article updates a story published April 27, 2023, about flood risk in South Florida.

articles.title: Midterms’ ‘blue tsunami’ gives Congress and states an opportunity to take action on climate change – here’s what they could actually do
articles.author: Geoffrey Henderson, Assistant Professor of Environmental Policy and Sustainability, University of Michigan
paras: The 2026 U.S. midterm elections are sweeping Democratic majorities into Congress and state legislatures across the country. That’s creating an opportunity to shift the country back to responding to climate change.
But faced with a president who staunchly opposes policies that could help slow climate change, what will these leaders with newfound power actually be able to do?

Democrats in Congress will have a stronger hand to play in their negotiations with the White House come January, and they may have leverage in pursuing climate policies during negotiations over the federal budget. Yet for the next two years, their ability to enact comprehensive climate legislation will likely be limited by President Donald Trump’s promised veto.

Beyond the federal level, six states – Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin – will have new Democratic trifectas: Democratic governors and Democratic majorities in both chambers of the legislature. These state trifectas create a chance to enact policies to advance clean energy and respond to voters’ concerns about energy affordability.
We study the politics and policies around climate change. Here are some ways we see potential for real change.
What can Congress do to restore clean energy spending?
When he took office in January 2025, Trump refused to spend money that Congress had appropriated for clean energy. The courts ruled that the move was illegal.

A few months later, Trump’s federal budget bill eliminated tax credits for producing wind power, investing in solar power and purchasing electric vehicles. It also cut other clean energy provisions of the Inflation Reduction Act, despite the law overwhelmingly benefiting Republican-held districts.
The new Democratic Congress will have authority over taxing and spending, known as the “power of the purse.”

U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, a Democrat from Maine who serves on the House Appropriations Committee, plans to withhold funding for federal agencies if the administration does not spend funds allocated to clean energy. Further, advocates believe Democrats can leverage budget negotiations with the White House to restore wind and solar tax credits.
How can Congress respond to federal agencies’ anti-environmental stances?

In his second term, Trump has doubled down on his wide-ranging effort to eliminate environmental regulations. His administration has handed out exemptions from air pollution rules to many facilities, including 71 coal-fired power plants. The administration has also intervened in permitting, holding up hundreds of wind and solar power projects.

Congressional majorities have the power to exercise oversight of federal agencies, including the ability to subpoena documents. They can use this authority to investigate the administration’s refusals both to enforce environmental regulations and to spend money allocated for clean energy.
Since Congress has limited legal means to force the administration to comply with investigations, its oversight powers give it leverage largely through bad press and lower approval ratings for Trump.

Congress has seen some movement lately on legislation that could boost renewable energy. A proposed bipartisan permitting reform bill could speed up construction of electricity transmission lines and clean energy sources such as wind, solar and geothermal power.

However, many climate advocates oppose the bill for accelerating fossil fuel projects and weakening environmental laws. For instance, opponents warn that the bill removes checks on environmentally harmful projects. U.S. Rep. Jared Huffman, a Democrat from California, has called for the new Congress to renegotiate the legislation.
What can state governments do to slow climate change?
Former Washington Gov. Jay Inslee, a Democrat, contends that “almost every (climate) policy you can think of … can be done at a state level.”

In recent years, unified Democratic control has allowed Michigan and Minnesota to pass ambitious climate laws, such as policies requiring that 100% of electricity comes from clean energy sources by 2040. Both are back under Democratic control, and incoming governors Jocelyn Benson and Amy Klobuchar each campaigned on expanding renewable energy.
Those and other states with new trifectas can now enact legislation that has been stalled for years due to partisan opposition.

In Pennsylvania, for example, Democratic lawmakers have advanced proposals that would allow community solar power, regulate data centers – these are huge electricity users – and require utilities to store excess electricity. But those proposals stalled under Republican control of the state Senate. That could change with Democrats gaining a trifecta.

Democrats also broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas. Given Texas’ burgeoning wind industry and solar power potential, a shift in its energy policy could help to significantly reduce emissions. Texas’ renewable energy requirements once drove wind power expansion. But electric utilities successfully pushed for weakening the law’s targets for solar power, and the state’s Republican government repealed the policy in 2023.

While Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa in Texas has focused more on affordable energy than renewable energy, she supports wind and solar power as a means of lowering energy costs. Advocates believe her victory will prevent the enactment of two proposed bills that would impose administrative hurdles and fines on renewable energy generators.

Unlike his predecessor, Ken Paxton, incoming Attorney General Nathan Johnson has signaled that he will not bring Texas into litigation against progressive federal policies such as environmental regulations.
Climate policies are broadly popular with Americans, though less so among Republicans. They are more popular than most people and politicians think.

In recent ballot measures, such as Nevada’s 50% renewable energy target in 2020 and Washington state’s cap-and-trade repeal effort in 2024, voters have favored climate policy. However, many Americans currently rate other priorities, such as healthcare, the economy and lowering high prices, as more important.

Taken together, this polling data suggests that bold climate actions may be more likely to flop among voters if they are seen as worsening other issues that voters care about. For example, if voters worry that climate legislation will increase costs, they may be less likely to support the politicians behind it.

In contrast, if politicians can reassure voters that their climate policies are complementary to addressing other public concerns, such action may be less likely to backfire and could even boost politicians’ popularity – even potentially among Republican voters. U.S. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democrat from Rhode Island, argues that Democrats should explain how renewable energy can lower electricity prices – a current priority for voters.
Looking back, looking ahead

Democrats arguably owe their newfound power to Trump’s unpopularity and widespread concerns about high prices. Their challenge will be to follow through on their promises to make voters’ lives more affordable. Policies promoting clean energy could be one vehicle for delivering that change.

articles.title: Electric cooking could be as important as EVs in the global energy transition
articles.author: Ed Brown, Professor of Global Energy Challenges, STEER Centre, Geography Department, Loughborough University
paras: Electric vehicles (EVs) have become the poster child for the green transition. Governments are investing billions in charging infrastructure. Manufacturers are transforming their production lines. Electrifying transport is a central pillar of climate policy.
But there is another potentially enormous driver of electrification that deserves attention: cooking.

I’m currently at the UN climate summit, Cop31 in Turkey, with my colleague Alicia Butterfield. As global manager of the Global Electric Cooking Coalition, she works with governments, development agencies and clean energy organisations to replace polluting traditional stoves with clean, electric cooking appliances.

We have been struck by how many researchers, government representatives and international organisations at this Cop are advocating for electric cooking to be included as a major component of the global energy transition. The question is no longer simply whether we can cook with electricity, but on how doing so can transform electricity systems, stimulate investment and accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels and polluting traditional cooking fuels.

The comparison with EVs is particularly interesting. Not everyone drives a car, but nearly everyone cooks. Cooking takes place in almost every household, as well as in restaurants, businesses, schools, hospitals and other institutions. It is a universal and essential energy service.

If EVs can become a major driver of electricity demand, why should electric cooking not play an equally important role? In terms of the number of people and institutions electric cooking can involve, it could have an even greater reach than electric transport.

Africa is already undergoing rapid electrification. Mission 300, an initiative funded by the World Bank and African Development Bank, aims to connect 300 million people in sub-Saharan Africa to electricity by 2030. Across the continent, electric cooking can help make electricity systems more economically sustainable over the longer term.

For national utilities, increased electricity consumption creates additional revenue. This can improve the commercial viability of investments in electricity generation and distribution networks. For decentralised electricity providers, including mini-grid operators, reliable demand from cooking can improve the return on investment. It can also make off-grid rural electrification projects more financially viable, potentially lowering tariffs for customers.

Of course, this is not a simple process. Adding large cooking loads can increase pressure on grids at evening peak points. Promoting institutional and commercial electric cooking provides a daytime load (higher demand) which can actually help to smooth demand across a 24-hour period. Some innovative approaches are being developed around differential time-of-day tariffs that encourage use of electricity at times of low demand. This can help “smooth demand”.

This transition can happen in many ways. In urban and semi-urban areas, households with grid connections are trialling electric pressure cookers, induction hobs and other efficient appliances. When they do so, the cost of their daily cooking often falls.

But connection to a national grid isn’t essential for energy access. In remote unconnected rural communities, electric cooking can be supported through decentralised renewable energy systems. The economics of adoption in these communities can be more difficult, especially if people are cooking with wood they collected themselves for free.

Research highlights that the costs of traditional biomass (such as wood and charcoal) extend beyond direct fuel expenditure. Costs include the considerable time, physical effort and opportunity costs associated with collecting, transporting and preparing firewood.

So with the right price point, electric cooking can be attractive even where firewood is freely collected. Reducing the time and drudgery of fuel collection can free up time for income-generating activities and other productive uses.

Advances in solar panels, battery storage and energy-efficient appliances, particularly electric pressure cookers, are improving the technical and economic feasibility of off-grid electric cooking. Innovative financial arrangements, frequently supported via carbon finance (incentivising carbon emissions reductions), are driving down appliance costs for the customer.

Cop31’s 35-by-35 global electrification pledge seeks to increase electricity’s share of global final energy consumption from around 23% today to 35% by 2035. This pledge is not yet a commitment, and at the time of writing, it remains far from clear what kind of an agreement will be reached.

Achieving this ambition requires more electricity generation (from renewables if electrification is going to drive accelerated climate action). It also relies on stronger grids and improved energy storage.
It needs a greater focus on the uses of electricity. The electrification of transport, buildings and industry is essential – so too is cooking.

These discussions demonstrate that cooking is increasingly being considered within national energy planning and international investment conversations. There is an important gap: electricity generation and grid infrastructure are often financed separately from the activities that create demand for that electricity.

Progress in Tanzania shows how electric cooking can help bridge that gap. In one remarkable high-level session organised by Sustainable Energy for All (an international initiative hosted by the UN) and the government of Tanzania, delegates heard directly from Samia Suluhu Hassan, Tanzania’s president. She outlined how the country is advancing its energy transition, partly by prioritising clean cooking in schools and health facilities.

Tanzania’s national clean cooking strategy aims for at least 80% of its population to use clean cooking solutions by 2034. Now in its third year, the UK-funded eCooking Scale and Support programme has worked with the Tanzanian energy ministry to encourage the adoption of electric cooking among households, institutions and businesses across the country.

This programme has introduced innovative financial approaches. These include utility on-bill financing of electric cooking appliances (whereby households repay upfront costs through monthly bills) and credit lines (a flexible borrowing agreement) for new appliance suppliers.

In school kitchens, polluting stoves (those that burn wood or charcoal) have been replaced with clean electric ones. New repair and maintenance training programmes have been introduced for electric cooking appliances. In collaboration with the Tanzania Bureau of Standards, new standards have been set for electric cooking appliances.

The programme demonstrates how under strong government vision and leadership, electricity utilities, financial institutions, appliance suppliers and development partners can work together to build an effective functioning electric cooking market.

Energy security is another powerful driver of the move towards locally generated renewable electricity. Reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels and volatile international energy markets makes the case for developing domestic electricity resources even stronger.

Scaling up electric cooking reduces harmful pollution from methane (a potent greenhouse gas with strong links to respiratory health problems) and microscopic particles of black carbon or soot (a short-lived climate pollutant). Moving away from polluting combustion-based cooking can deliver important climate and public health benefits alongside carbon dioxide reductions.

For more households to switch to electric cooking, appliances must be affordable, electricity supplies reliable and people must know what options are available. This electrification transition must be designed around local circumstances and addressed through coordinated policy, investment and innovation. If policymakers look beyond the most visible technologies, cooking could be placed firmly on Cop31’s global electrification agenda.

Ed Brown leads UK Aid's Modern Energy Cooking Services programme (funded via the UK's FCDO under their Ayrton programme). Research that he leads is also currently funded by UKRI and the Climate and Clean Air Coalition.

articles.title: Expect to see fewer and smaller potatoes this Christmas – it’s the ‘worst harvest since 1950s’
articles.author: Robin Gowers, Senior Lecturer at the Writtle School of Agriculture, Animal and Environmental Sciences, Anglia Ruskin University
paras: Britain’s potato harvest this winter could be one of the smallest in decades.

This is partly down to the hot summer and a poor growing year. Potatoes have shallow roots and need steady moisture, so dry spells cut yield and size. Where farmers had stored water to regularly irrigate, crops fared better.

With 75% of England in drought in September, and Wales also affected by dry conditions, one model estimated that British potato yields would be 11% below average. It used the 2018 harvest as a guide. Some farmers reported a greater than 50% drop in how many potatoes they were harvesting.
Wholesale prices had already risen by more than 40% by early August. By September, big British buyers were reportedly paying more than £300 a tonne for potatoes.
The Food and Drink Federation has warned of the worst potato harvest since the 1950s.

Growers have warned supermarkets to expect smaller potatoes and tighter supplies this year, so shoppers may need to accept wider variation in size and quality. This is partly because other European countries, which often provide supplies to the UK, suffered the same hot summer, and this affected their crops, too.

But shoppers may not feel the full effect of higher wholesale prices this winter. Potatoes are more likely to become significantly more expensive next year. It is also worth noting that many supermarkets subsidise potato prices.

Lidl has announced that a 2kg bag will cost 9p in the week before Christmas. The supermarket says it is funding the low price itself, so this price tells shoppers nothing about what the crop costs to grow.
Supermarkets agree prices and volumes with farmers well in advance. Retailers may absorb some of the higher costs this year rather than risk losing customers to competitors.
The bigger question is whether British farmers will carry on planting Britain’s favourite vegetable in future, and what happens if more decide it is no longer worth the risk.
In 2025, the issue was too many potatoes heading for shops – the UK produced 5.5 million tonnes, 8.5% more than the year before. This caused prices paid to farmers to collapse.

By February 2026, top-quality maris piper potatoes were fetching about £180 a tonne on the open market, less than half the £400 of a year earlier. Contract prices for the following year were also weaker.
Growers did what economics predicts: they planted less. Analysts put this year’s area in Great Britain at around 101,000 hectares, well below the 117,500 recorded in 2020.
Then came the heat and drought.
Why can’t farmers cash in?

Higher prices should encourage farmers to plant more. But a price spike helps only those with potatoes to sell at open-market rates. Most crops are grown under contract, and growers who struggle to deliver the agreed tonnage or quality may miss out.
Some big buyers that normally rely on contracts are buying open-market potatoes as fast as they can, so growers with uncommitted crops may do well.
Meanwhile, costs for farmers keep climbing. Conflict in the Middle East has pushed up energy and fertiliser costs. Labour and machinery are also more expensive.

Meanwhile, the end of the basic payment scheme (an annual payment for farmers that followed environmental guidelines) and controversies about its replacements may have removed a financial cushion that once helped farms through bad years.

The potato contract price is fixed in advance, so growers have little room to pass costs on. Tighter margins are also hitting buyers, packers and processors, but it is growers that carry the bulk of the weather risk.

Economists call this pattern the cobweb cycle. In the textbook version, farmers plant according to last season’s price, so a glut leads to a price crash, then cuts in planting, then shortage and high prices, then over-planting again. Potatoes have followed this familiar cycle almost to the letter this year.

Yet several forces pull the other way. Speaking before the summer’s hot weather and drought, in May, Scott Walker, chief executive of the industry body representing the potato sector, GB Potatoes, said that many growers were weighing up how much exposure they would carry into 2027. The body has warned that growers could leave the business or reduce their crop.

Contract prices were weaker this year, costs are higher, and drought has shown how exposed the crop is. Depressed cereal markets offer little alternative income, so a wholesale exit is not certain either.
Farmers will be looking closely at what supermarkets offer them in 2027. High open market prices alone will not bring growers back.

Two things matter most: the contracts offered this winter, and whether farmers can secure water supplies for next summer. Signs are that water access may remain tight. For instance, the Environment Agency put England’s reservoirs at only 54% of capacity in early October. Higher prices could prompt a rebound in planting, but a normal-weather harvest could tip the market back into glut, forcing prices down again.
Will British farmers stop planting potatoes?

In September 2026, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs saw no indication that winter supplies were at risk but added that it was too early to assess the drought’s full impact on potato production and that there was, at that point, no indication that winter potato supplies were at risk. Registered potato farmer numbers fell from about 2,466 in 2000 to 1,611 in 2020, when the statutory body collating data on potato farmers was discontinued. But each bad year pushes more to ask whether the crop is worth it.

Tim Rooke, National Farmers’ Union potato policy group chair, said in 2025 that the UK imports approximately 1 million tonnes of frozen chips a year, because the risk against return on investment of growing potatoes is astronomically high.

A food system that leaves a shrinking number of growers to absorb the weather and price risk should not be surprised when they plant less. One option could be fairer contracts that share risk, and investment in water storage. But less certain supply chains and more volatile prices could cost shoppers more.
Climate change means water shortages and high temperatures will happen more often across Europe. Potato farmers are, therefore, likely to face these challenges more regularly in the future.

articles.title: Dunkelflaute: why cloudy, windless weather is a challenge for power networks that rely on renewables
articles.author: David Brayshaw, Professor in Climate Science and Energy Meteorology, University of Reading
paras: In early November 2024, a large mass of still, cloudy, cold air settled over much of north-west Europe. For much of a week, wind turbines barely moved and the output from solar farms was negligible. In some areas, cold temperatures meant people needed extra electricity to heat their homes.

Something similar happened on a smaller scale in early November 2026, when low wind-power generation across Europe left the UK scrambling for extra electricity. These are examples of a so-called dunkelflaute, German for “dark doldrums”, a weather-related challenge for electricity systems as they become increasingly reliant on renewables. Wind and solar generation now accounts for more than a third of the electricity produced in Great Britain, for example, from a baseline of almost nothing just 20 years ago. This shift is central to efforts to reach net zero, and will play a key role in decarbonising other sectors such as heating and transport.

The introduction of large amounts of weather-sensitive generation has created new challenges for power-system operators. A central concept within this is “balancing” – the need to ensure the supply of and demand for electricity match in near real-time.

This used to be relatively simple. When demand increased, power plants would burn more coal or gas. These days, maintaining balance can be extremely challenging in periods of unfavourable weather conditions and, if left unchecked, mismatches in supply and demand could quickly spiral into disconnections and blackouts.
Putting power systems under pressure

A dunkelflaute is usually associated with high-pressure weather systems over north-western Europe. As these move slowly and cover large areas, their effects can persist across several countries for days at a time, reducing the availability of wind and solar power simultaneously.

In winter, these high-pressure systems are typically associated with colder temperatures in northern Europe, thereby driving up the demand for electricity. This combination of reduced renewable generation and higher demand puts individual power systems under strain.

The overall impact is exacerbated when neighbouring countries experience the same conditions at the same time, limiting opportunities to import electricity to compensate. As these events can last several days, electricity storage can become depleted – particularly given that current storage capacity is typically designed to provide power for several hours at most.
How electricity systems can cope

Power systems can cope with dunkelflaute conditions in several ways. At present, as many countries are still transitioning away from fossil fuels, a common approach has been to use existing power stations as a backup.

Gas power stations, for example, can adjust their output relatively quickly to match changes in demand and renewable generation. This makes them a convenient way to maintain supply during a dunkelflaute, though it can be expensive, especially when the supply-demand balancing act is very tight. The UK National Energy System Operator’s Clean Power 2030 advice proposes keeping around 35GW of gas power to provide backup when renewable generation is low.

In the longer term, power-system operators and planners may seek to make electricity systems more flexible, reducing the need to match generation and demand instantaneously. Several measures can help to do this, and some are already in use.

Electricity use can be shifted to times when the weather is favourable, for instance, perhaps by offering lower prices during windy or sunny days. Strengthening transmission connections within and between countries also helps to make better use of regional differences in renewable generation and electricity demand.

Building more electricity storage could also help absorb surplus generated electricity and release it when supplies are low, from large batteries to alternatives such as pumped storage hydropower which works by moving water between two reservoirs. Linking electricity systems with other forms of energy use could help here. For example, excess electricity could be used to produce hydrogen, which can then be stored and used as a fuel.

Understanding the severity, geographical extent and duration of dunkelflaute conditions, and the extent to which they may affect electricity supplies, is therefore an important challenge, both in the present and under a changing climate.

However, it is worth remembering that dunkelflaute periods were only identified as a significant risk to power systems because of the growing reliance on wind and solar energy. Before these technologies became widespread, few would have considered these otherwise benign conditions to be a weather hazard compared to more familiar threats such as flooding or storms.

This underlines the importance of being alert to emerging weather risks as energy systems evolve, and for more collaboration between energy and climate researchers. This collaboration will be essential to managing weather risks as renewable energy becomes the norm and the climate keeps changing.

David Brayshaw has worked on research projects with a variety of funders, including UKRI NERC, the UK government, and the energy industry. He is currently seconded part-time as an advisor to Ofgem. Any views he expresses are as an independent researcher at the University of Reading.

articles.title: Cop31 climate summit debates how fossil fuel subsidies have hidden costs on nature
articles.author: Benjamin Selwyn, Professor of International Relations and International Development, Department of International Relations, University of Sussex
paras: As world leaders gather at the UN climate summit, Cop31, in Turkey, one issue has returned to the centre of climate politics: subsidies. Brazil has renewed calls for countries to phase out fossil-fuel subsidies, while campaigners and several governments argue that public money should no longer support industries driving climate change.

The debate is usually framed quite simply. Governments spend billions reducing the cost of producing or consuming coal, oil and gas. Remove those subsidies, and the transition to cleaner energy will accelerate.
But this focus on visible subsidies obscures a much larger one.

More than 70 years ago, the political economist Karl William Kapp argued that modern economies depend on a vast invisible subsidy – the systematic transfer of social and environmental costs onto society and nature.

Published in 1950, his book The Social Costs of the Business Enterprise argued that environmental degradation, public health harms and resource depletion are not merely unfortunate by-products of economic growth. Rather, they are inseparable from a market system organised around private profit and competitive cost reduction.

Mainstream economics describes such harms as “externalities” that arise when markets fail to reflect all relevant costs. Kapp, by contrast, argued that pollution, ecological degradation and ill health were recurring outcomes of an economic system in which market prices systematically exclude many of the real costs of production.

Kapp’s argument was that the market mechanism itself rewards economic activities that can offload part of their costs onto workers, communities, public budgets and ecosystems. Cost-shifting is not the exception but a foundational means through which competitive market economies reproduce themselves.

From this perspective, subsidies extend beyond tax breaks, preferential loans and direct government support. The deeper subsidy arises when economic activity proceeds without accounting for its full social and ecological costs.

The climate crisis provides an obvious example. Fossil fuels appear relatively cheap because many of their costs, including air pollution, ecological degradation and climate disruption, are borne elsewhere.
Recent attempts to place monetary values on environmental damage, although developed for very different purposes, lend support to Kapp’s argument.

Paradoxically, many of these initiatives were designed to integrate nature more fully into economic calculation and investment decisions, yet their findings reveal the extent to which profitability depends on costs that remain outside market accounts.

One 2024 industry report found that the environmental costs associated with cereal-grain cultivation in eastern Asia were almost three times greater than the revenues generated by the sector. Similar patterns appeared across crop cultivation in southern Asia and South America. In many cases, environmental damages exceeded revenues. This indicates that if these costs were fully borne within production, many companies in this part of the agricultural economy could not remain economically viable.
Comparable dynamics are visible across mining, chemicals and cement production, where estimated environmental damages also exceeded revenues.

The same pattern is, unsurprisingly, evident in fossil fuels. According to an International Monetary Fund estimate, the global underpricing of fossil fuels amounts to an industrial subsidy of roughly US$6.7 trillion (£5 trillion) annually. This figure includes climate damages, air pollution and other costs excluded from market prices. Rather than appearing on balance sheets, they are dispersed across societies and ecosystems.
The apparent profitability of major sectors of the global economy depends not simply on technological innovation or productive efficiency, but on the continuing ability to transfer costs elsewhere.

This reveals a contradiction at the heart of contemporary climate policy. At Cop31, governments are debating how to eliminate environmentally harmful subsidies while simultaneously encouraging private investment in the green transition. Yet both discussions often assume that markets merely require better incentives and more accurate pricing to align profit with sustainability.

Kapp argued that environmental destruction persists not because costs are poorly measured, but because economic success depends on excluding them from market calculations by shifting them onto society and nature.
Recalculating nature costs
The Cop31 debate over subsidies is important. It is right that social movements and progressive governments push for, and commit to, more renewable energy generation.

But it should also encourage climate-conscious people to think beyond subsidies that appear in government budgets. The larger question is whether an economy can genuinely be considered sustainable when many its costs are systematically transferred onto others.

Seventy-five years after Kapp first made the argument, climate breakdown, biodiversity loss and ecological instability suggest that the hidden subsidy to capital that he identified has become one of the defining features of this era.

The challenge is not only to remove public support from environmentally destructive activities while increasing investment in renewables. It is also to confront an economic system that treats society and nature as repositories for costs that markets refuse to count.

articles.title: How the US elections and Iran war are influencing the UN’s COP31 climate talks – and discussions around fossil fuels
articles.author: Jennifer Morgan, Senior Fellow, Center for International Environment and Resource Policy and Climate Policy Lab, Tufts University
paras: The 2026 United Nations climate talks are all about real-world impact. That’s evident as I listen to government officials and others from around the world at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.

World leaders are seeing their countries suffer from intensifying storms and heat fueled by climate change and from one of the worst global energy crises in history. A U.N. report found that global warming will overshoot 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), the level countries agreed a decade ago to try to avoid because of the growing risk of dangerous climate change.
The Middle East conflict has intensified oil and gas price and supply volatility, pushing economies to the brink as energy and food prices spike and energy security falters.
Countries that rely on imported fossil fuels for their energy sources have borne the brunt of the energy crisis. Those doubling down on renewable energy are weathering the crisis better.

In Pakistan, for example, the rapid expansion of solar power over the past six years helped the country avoid more than US$12 billion in fossil fuel imports before the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran began in February 2026. One forecast suggests solar could save the country more than $6 billion more by the end of the year. Spain, which relies less on natural gas and more on solar energy for electricity than most European countries, kept electricity prices lower and avoided the worst of the gas-driven spikes seen in more exposed systems such as Italy’s.

In formal negotiations and in meetings around the U.N.’s broader Global Climate Action Agenda, countries are working on ways to accelerate the use of clean energy and to provide poorer countries with the resources to adapt to climate change and expand clean energy.

I have been following international climate negotiations for years as a former special climate envoy for Germany and senior fellow at the Fletcher School at Tufts University. In 2026, after two years of the Trump administration’s pressure to get countries to abandon efforts to slow climate change, I’m seeing rising concern among leaders about the costs of fossil fuels on economies and people’s lives.
The electrification solution

A step in transitioning away from fossil fuels is shifting to electrification powered by clean energy. The co-presidents of COP31, from Turkey and Australia, have proposed a global target of 35% of all energy use coming from electricity by 2035 – including for transportation and industry – and they are working to persuade other countries to sign on.

Hitting that 35% mark could save fossil-fuel-importing countries $400 billion a year, according to the International Energy Agency. In consumer terms, $100 spent on electricity powers a car up to three times farther than $100 of gasoline, based on global averages. Reaching the goal could slash energy emissions across transportation, buildings and industry by up to 55% by 2035.

However, the source of electrification matters. Forecasts from the International Renewable Energy Agency show that at least 78% of the electricity powering the world must come from renewable energy sources to keep global warming under the 1.5 C limit. Electrification delivers for both the climate and energy security if it runs on clean power instead of energy from oil, gas and coal.
Getting the world to that point will require addressing some key barriers: the cost of infrastructure needed to deliver clean energy and the need for policies to encourage the changes.

Beyond the formal negotiations, countries are discussing multiple initiatives to provide technical support to one another, as countries develop power grids that can manage the variability of solar and wind power, and financial help to countries that need it.
Voters show their frustration with fossil fuels

The high financial and environmental costs of fossil fuels have been reshaping global politics. Voters came out in big numbers over the past few months to elect leaders who support clean, affordable energy solutions.
The world saw this notably with the reelection of Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and the biggest Democratic congressional victory in the United States in over three decades.

Lula, in his first international trip after winning his fourth term, called on the COP31 presidents to carry forward Brazil’s work as host of COP30 on a transition away from fossil fuels. He announced that Brazil will host a future conference on the fossil fuel transition, following the first in Colombia in April 2026 and a second planned in 2027 in the island nation of Tuvalu.

Brazil has clearly emerged as a climate superpower in Antalya. With its greatest one-year reduction in deforestation and its leadership in producing three plans, known as road maps, to help the world transition away from fossil fuels, end deforestation and provide the $1.3 trillion in financing needed for developing countries, Brazil has demonstrated it understands the urgency of the climate crisis.
We will see whether the co-presidents of COP31 will answer the calls from Lula and U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres to support these road maps becoming formal guidance for all countries.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom and a delegation of 18 members of the U.S. House of Representatives also came to COP31 to signal the presence of American leadership on future climate policy. President Donald Trump has pulled the U.S. out of the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change, the Paris Agreement and dozens of other international organizations and treaties. The U.S. did not send a formal delegation to the climate talks.
As former U.S. climate envoy John Kerry said in Antalya, “Americans did vote for clean, affordable energy, and they also voted for clean governance.”

The international community will be watching to see whether the newly elected Democratic majority in Congress can help safeguard U.S. climate science after the Trump administration’s extensive funding cuts, and whether it will restore critical funding to international efforts dealing with climate change.

At COP31, the shift in the real-world politics of energy has dominated several events and the formal negotiations. But the countries that are likely to lose from such a transition are also working diligently to slow this transition. On the opening day, a coalition of oil-producing countries led by Saudi Arabia announced it opposed any mention of Brazil’s road map away from fossil fuels in the official COP31 agreement.

For COP31 to be a success, the diplomatic process must demonstrate that it can catch up to the real economy and meet this moment of energy and climate crisis. I believe the summit’s final agreement should accelerate the electrification of infrastructure around the world and, at the same time, drive the transition away from fossil fuels in order to protect global security, economic stability and everyday citizens.

Jennifer Morgan does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Annual water-quality reports don’t tell the full story of what you’re drinking
articles.author: Sarah Glass, Ph.D. Candidate in Civil and Environmental Engineering, Rice Water Institute, Rice University
paras: Water is vital to life, which is part of why we study what’s in it.

Drinking water isn’t just H₂O – though there are over 15 septillion molecules of it in a standard glass. It also contains natural minerals, dissolved organic and biological matter, and substances that enter from agriculture, industry, consumer products and water treatment.

Most of these substances are harmless at the concentrations typically found in water. Some are beneficial, and even essential, such as sodium, fluoride and calcium ions, which build strong bones and teeth. Additionally, these ions balance electrolytes that regulate bodily function.

In fact, drinking large quantities of completely demineralized or distilled water can disrupt the body’s electrolyte balance. This water would dilute the natural sodium levels in blood, potentially causing hyponatremia, a condition with symptoms such as nausea, headache, confusion and seizures.

Most people encounter water-quality science through an annual report from their local water company. It’s usually a couple of pages long with chemical names and numbers in a table. It lists various compounds that may exist in the water, summarizes what has been found in tests of the water source, and explains whether the water meets government-set standards that promote and protect public health and safety.
These reports provide important information about drinking water safety, but they are not a complete inventory of every substance scientists can detect or are working to understand.

We study a range of contaminants, chemical and biological, that are found in drinking water, with the goal of developing technologies to further safeguard public health. This includes pollutants and pathogens that are not included on an annual water report.
A secret world of sneaky water pollutants

Consider perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances, more commonly known as PFAS and also called “forever chemicals” because they persist in the environment for a long time. These are a large family of chemicals used in consumer products because they resist water, oil and heat.
Research has linked exposure to certain PFAS with adverse chronic health effects, such as endocrine disruption, low birth weight in fetuses and certain types of cancer.

Federal drinking water standards now limit the amount of two common types of PFAS found in the environment to 4 parts per trillion, a level extremely hard to detect even on advanced analytical equipment. However, the broader chemical family includes many others whose occurrence and health effects are less understood by scientists and completely missed by the public or policy.

The challenge that water-quality engineers face is not simply to determine whether PFAS, or other compounds and pollutants, are present. Rather, researchers need to understand the concentrations of those chemicals in the water, how people are exposed to them, what their effects on the body are, and how effectively different treatment technologies can remove or destroy them.
What doesn’t kill you … might later

Pharmaceutical residues from medicine that passes through people’s bodies enter sewage systems. Agricultural chemicals such as pesticides flow off croplands into waterways. Both of these types of waste can break down into new, less studied compounds as they move through soil and water, eventually collecting in groundwater or wastewater to be treated and redistributed. The potential long-term effects of these lesser-studied compounds are not fully understood.

Water treatment plants often use chlorine as part of the disinfection process. But when chlorine reacts with natural organic matter, such as decayed plants and microorganisms, it forms disinfection byproducts. These byproducts include chemicals such as trihalomethanes, which are known carcinogens that must be removed with further treatment before the water is safe to drink.

Some contaminants pose an immediate threat; others pose threats that accumulate over time. For instance, ingesting microplastics in drinking water may not hurt you right now, but they are being detected in people’s blood years after exposure. We water-quality scientists want to know not only what’s in the water, but what it might do to your body right away or across decades.
Bad to drink, even worse to breathe

The timescale and route of exposure of waterborne contaminants matter, too. If stagnant pipes are left unused for a long time, bacteria can build up. Then, when people start a shower or an outdoor fountain, that bacteria travels into the air in mist. This poses a different kind of threat than exposure to a chemical pollutant in drinking water because this would lead to bacteria infection.

For example, when there is a large buildup of Legionella spp. , a group of bacteria that can grow in drinking water distribution systems and power plant cooling towers when condensation pools, people who inhale the water vapor can develop Legionnaires’ disease, an acute form of pneumonia. Waterborne pathogens and their associated infections account for billions of dollars in maintenance and healthcare costs annually.
Hazards, risk and Flint as an example

Moreover, it is important to distinguish what is hazardous and how it could eventually become a human health risk. In the case of Flint, Michigan, lead in a water pipe is a hazard, but as long as the water flowing through it is chemically stable and doesn’t react with lead from the pipes, the immediate risk to human health is low.

In the city’s 2014 water crisis, water from a new source was not chemically treated to reduce its ability to pick up lead from the pipes. By 2016, people had been ordered not to drink the water anymore because it was contaminated with dangerous levels of lead, which can cause neurological problems and impair brain function.

The real questions go beyond just looking at what’s in water, to include what kinds of dangers are there, whether immediate like Legionnaires’ disease or chronic like lead poisoning or cancer. Regulatory standards don’t always address every potential source or type of contamination.
The next time you review your local water report, don’t just look at what is being monitored; consider what may not be on the list at all.
