articles.title: Wealthy countries aren’t protected from climate extremes – Europe must adapt quickly too
articles.author: Joshua Garland, Postdoctoral Research Associate, Environmental Change, Lund University
paras: Extreme heatwaves across Europe led to significant annual deaths this summer. In Spain, floods in Valencia during 2024 killed 200 people and paralysed infrastructure. Germany’s 2021 floods highlighted severe weaknesses in early-warning communication, while wildfires in France led to large-scale evacuations and reduced air quality.

It’s easy to assume that strong institutions and technological capacity protect wealthy countries from the consequences of climate change. But evidence suggests otherwise. Well-resourced cities remain vulnerable to rapid-onset extremes. Our research across high-income countries identifies a fundamental challenge here: adaptation responsibility is frequently fragmented across governance levels.

The knock-on effects of climate-induced extremes also expose longstanding inequalities between people of different ages, genders and race, for example. Migrant, elderly and low-income communities are disproportionately affected by climate consequences. This is not simply because these communities are more exposed to the effects of extreme weather. Their vulnerabilities are also shaped by housing quality, income, health and lower political influence.

At international climate negotiations, such as the UN climate summit Cop31, adaptation is traditionally framed as something wealthy countries finance and poorer countries need. There are compelling historical and ethical reasons for this. This framing can nonetheless obscure another important reality: adaptation is a challenge for every country.
Wealth does not guarantee adaptation

In the UK, older homes are vulnerable to heat and cold extremes, while coastal areas are exposed to climate-exacerbated flooding and erosion. In East Anglia, experiences of one of Europe’s fastest eroding coastlines has resulted in lost homes and risks to national energy infrastructure, with the Climate Change Committee emphasising inadequate adaptation progress.

In Sweden, confidence in strong institutions obscures vulnerabilities. Nordic exceptionalism restrains governments from publicly acknowledging climate risks and adaptation deficits, confounded by overconfidence in technology. With one of Europe’s oldest populations, new forms of immobility and uneven exposure to heatwaves are being created. Coastal communities face increasing flooding and erosion. And the Sami Indigenous peoples are losing their livelihoods as ecological losses impact reindeer herding.

While relocation may seem a straightforward adaptation solution, it can mean losing homes, livelihoods, cultural heritage and place connections that have shaped generations. This reveals further weaknesses in how adaptation is assessed. Governments report their progress through targets and resilience indicators, yet this often overlooks communities’ losses.
The problem is not that wealthy countries lack resources, but that resources do not automatically translate into effective protection.
Adaptation is a political problem

Adaptation is often presented as a technical challenge, by improving infrastructure or early warning systems. While essential, these measures are not sufficient and fragmented governance remains a key challenge.

In Sweden, municipalities carry responsibility for local adaptation but lack national support. In the UK, adaptation efforts driven by local authorities and agencies are constrained by national-level policies and budgets. Local authorities are expected to manage growing risks without the resources, powers or national support required to act.

The EU’s emerging Framework for Climate Resilience offers an opportunity to address these shortcomings. It acknowledges needs to strengthen Europe’s preparedness. Whether stronger EU ambitions will translate to effective action remains an important question. Without engaging directly with underlying governance challenges, resilience risks becoming a political, rather than lived, reality.

As governments gather for Cop31, acknowledging adaptation failures in wealthy countries should not become an argument for reducing support to others. Quite the opposite. Recognising inequalities within wealthy societies reinforces the principle that vulnerability is shaped by political and economic conditions, not simply GDP.

Protecting European communities and supporting adaptation elsewhere are both necessary. A lack of climate adaptation in wealthy countries expose a fundamental contradiction. Societies with substantial resources risk failing their citizens over foreseeable climate risks. Addressing this requires more than technologies and targets.

Acknowledging adaptation deficits is essential for advancing global and domestic climate justice. It helps explain why adaptation remains underfunded globally, why progress is uneven and why a more honest conversation is needed.

Wealthy countries must support adaptation elsewhere and confront domestic vulnerabilities. Otherwise, adaptation advances only on paper while exposure and inequality grow everywhere. The UN climate negotiation process offers opportunities to shift this conversation, but only by recognising that every country needs to adapt and that this is a collective task.

articles.title: What Scotland is getting wrong on recycling – and Wales is getting right
articles.author: Ian Williams, Professor of Applied Environmental Science, University of Southampton
paras: Scotland has ambitions to become an environmental leader, but its recycling rate has just fallen to a five-year low.

The Scottish household recycling rate fell from 44.3% in 2024 to 42.8% in 2025, according to recently released figures. These figures also show the levels vary widely across the country, with Glasgow one of the lowest local authorities at only 24% and Clackmannanshire at 56%. The Scottish government had previously set a recycling target of 70% of waste by 2025.

It is tempting to blame Scottish households. But research has shown recycling is shaped by social, cultural and structural conditions. Participation improves when services fit people’s everyday lives and make recycling convenient. People need authorities to provide suitable local infrastructure, services and behavioural support to enable effective recycling.

Scotland’s recycling services remain inconsistent and confusing. This is partly down to the continuing variation between local authority systems. Depending on where someone lives, there can be differences in which materials are accepted, container types and colours and whether glass is collected at the kerbside.
The wide variation between councils, from 18.2% to 56.5%, points to inconsistent services rather than individual attitudes alone.

Meanwhile, Scotland has struggled to introduce a return scheme for drinks containers, where a deposit is paid and then returned when recycled. Initially expected to start in October 2025, this has been postponed to October 2027, and will no longer include glass, due to wrangles with the UK government over devolved powers.
This was expected to raise recycling levels of eligible drinks containers to around 90%. A similar deposit scheme in Ireland has been very successful at pushing up recycling levels.

UK-wide figures also show a distinct difference between the four nations: Wales recycled 58.6% (up from 4.8% of household waste in 1998-99), Northern Ireland 50.1%, England 43.8% and Scotland comes bottom at 42.7% in 2024. These outcomes reflect political choices, not simply how diligently households sort their rubbish. Scotland’s lower rate reflects lack of access to convenient collection systems, cost barriers, limited reprocessing capacity and increasing incineration of recyclables.
Overall, recycling has stalled across England, Scotland and Northern Ireland while incineration of waste has expanded.
The municipal rate of recycling has increased to 68.4% in 2024-25. Municipal waste includes all local-authority-collected waste, including some commercial waste, street sweepings and litter bins.
But Wales shows that stagnation in recycling levels is not inevitable, and the nation has become a global leader on this front.

This reflects a sustained Welsh government policy, reinforced in 2021 with a new approach that set statutory local authority targets, invested in collections, as well as monitoring and political backing. Wales also imposed a moratorium on new large-scale energy-from-waste developments in 2021.

The Welsh system is not perfect. Its municipal rate remained below the 70% national target for 2024-25. Nevertheless, 20 of its 22 local authorities improved, demonstrating what sustained institutional pressure can achieve. Its experience suggests that targets work best when they are backed by infrastructure, accountability and stable long-term policy.
The first UK recycling in the early 2000s focused on relatively accessible materials such as paper, glass, metals and garden waste.
But further progress depends on addressing food waste, plastic films, textiles, electrical products and complex packaging.

These streams are harder to collect, separate and process, while markets for some recovered materials, where waste is reused, remain uncertain. Variable quality, volatile prices and weak demand for some materials increase costs and risk, potentially leaving councils without buyers.

Another reason recycling have not climbed as high as predicted is that people cannot recycle materials that councils do not collect. To help people recycle more it is important to eliminate confusing labels, redesign packaging that was never designed to be recycled or create new markets for recovered materials.

It’s important to note that landfill reduction is also an important environmental achievement, and in Scotland, for instance, landfill use has declined – down 82.5% since 2011 – although incineration has increased. In 2024 1.86 million tonnes was incinerated, an increase of 239,000 tonnes (14.7%) from 2023. Poorly managed landfill sites can pollute soil and water, release methane and require monitoring long after closure. The 1999 EU Landfill Directive, landfill tax, statutory targets and kerbside collections helped transform the system.

But the UK is increasingly burning what it no longer wants to bury. In 2024, 63 energy-from-waste plants burned 16.8 million tonnes of residual waste. Since 2024, there are ten incinerators under construction in England and two in Scotland, but none in Wales and Northern Ireland. As people recycle more there’s less need for these, so why are so many being built?

For non-recyclable waste, modern incineration may be preferable to landfill. It reduces waste volume and can generate electricity or heat. But it is controversial. Incineration is the dirtiest way the UK generates power. It emits carbon and causes smells as well as destroying materials that could otherwise remain in use. It also often causes nearby residents to worry about health risks.

In 2024, 82.3% of Scottish household waste classified as “other diversion from landfill” was managed through incineration. Landfilled household waste fell by 37.7%, but the quantity managed through “other diversion” rose by 16.1%. Scotland is therefore managing its residual waste differently, but without achieving an equivalent improvement in waste prevention or recovering or reusing materials.
The UK’s reduction in how much waste it deposits into landfill was the first waste revolution. The next change must be preventing waste and keeping products and materials in use for longer.

Governments should ensure residual waste contracts do not penalise councils for reducing rubbish. They should reward durable, repairable and genuinely recyclable products. Priority should be given to food, flexible plastics, textiles, electrical equipment and complex packaging.

Wales shows that sustained recycling progress is also possible. The next waste revolution will begin when conserving materials takes priority over finding another way to destroy them. Those in Scotland who want the country to take an environmental leadership role should take note.

articles.title: Oceans and forests have absorbed roughly half our carbon emissions for decades, slowing climate change – but can they keep it up?
articles.author: Andrew C. Manning, Visiting Professor of Carbon Cycle Science, Rochester Institute of Technology
paras: Over the past two centuries, humans have pumped billions of tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere by burning fossil fuels, raising global temperatures in the process.
Luckily for humanity, Earth has done what it could to soften the impact.
The world’s oceans have absorbed 35% of carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels since 1990, our new research shows, and the forests and other plants of the world have absorbed another 13%.

The importance of these two enormous natural carbon sinks cannot be overstated as global temperatures rise, fueling heat waves, fires, storms, floods and droughts around the world. Yet there is much that scientists do not understand about these carbon sinks – most importantly, how exactly they’ll behave in the future.

If the oceans and forests keep absorbing the same amount of carbon dioxide, scientists will have a sense of what to expect in the future and what can be done to slow climate change. And governments will know their remaining carbon budgets – that is, how much carbon dioxide can still be emitted into the atmosphere while keeping global temperatures below agreed-to levels.
But what if those carbon sinks change?

We have been working on greenhouse gas measurements for decades. In a new study, published Nov. 12, 2026, in the journal Science, we describe an alternative method for measuring these crucial carbon sinks, and what it shows.

We found that while the ocean sink has been expanding, meaning the oceans are taking in more carbon dioxide, that expansion might begin to slow down, leaving the oceans less effective at absorbing carbon in the coming decades. We found that the land sink has not been expanding, which was something of a surprise.
The fiendishly difficult task of measuring carbon sinks
Measuring how much carbon is being taken up by the world’s oceans and forests is devilishly difficult and prohibitively expensive.

This is because many parts of the land and ocean don’t behave in the same ways. What occurs in one ocean region or forest can be very different from another; and the behavior in one year can be very different in the next, often for reasons scientists do not fully understand.

Computer models can help overcome some of these complexities, but they too have limitations. Satellites can also help, but they cannot see through clouds, nor can they see what is happening in the soil or mid-to-deep ocean.
As carbon cycle scientists, we set out to find a different way to measure these carbon sinks.

Our new study approaches the problem from another angle. We used high-precision measurements of atmospheric oxygen (O₂), combined with atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) measurements, to quantify how the ocean and land carbon sinks take up carbon dioxide.

This works because land, oceans and burning fossil fuels have different effects on oxygen: When fossil fuels are burned, they not only produce CO₂, they consume O₂. On land, when plants take up CO₂ to grow, they simultaneously release O₂. When the oceans take up atmospheric CO₂, there is no corresponding release of O₂.

This means that if we measure both CO₂ and O₂ in the atmosphere, then we can quantify the ocean and land carbon sinks. It is a straightforward mathematical approach of solving two equations with two unknowns, combined with our knowledge and measurements of the global budgets of CO₂ and O₂.
When we looked at the ocean and land carbon sinks over the past three decades, the results were surprising and sobering.

In contrast to most computer model simulations, we did not find the land carbon sink increasing over time to keep pace with increasing fossil fuel emissions. We did, however, find a larger ocean carbon sink than predicted by most models, and we found that it has been increasing as emissions grow.
Where is the climate headed?

If these trends in carbon sinks continue, then in the coming decades, humans will be relying more heavily on the oceans to slow down climate change. But in the next few decades, there are reasons to believe the oceans could become less effective at absorbing carbon.

For example, warmer waters are not able to hold as much gas, such as carbon dioxide. Warmer surface waters are also less efficient at mixing into the deep ocean, which has the beneficial effect of locking carbon dioxide away from the atmosphere for many hundreds of years.
The data for the past decade hints at the possibility that while the ocean carbon sink is increasing now, its rate of increase may be slowing down.
Carbon cycle models need to improve

For the oceans, most computer models agree with each other, but, for the historical period, they do not match our oxygen-based results. For the land, models vary widely from each other, and most do not match our oxygen-based results.

Computer models are essential to provide governments with feasible scenarios to avoid dangerous climate change, but to be effective they need to be better grounded in what real-world observations are showing. Nature is difficult to represent with a series of equations, and observations are few considering the size of the planet.

We believe our study improves understanding of global carbon sinks and can help lead to more reliable projections of what might happen with climate change in the coming decades. But like any scientific approach, our oxygen method also has drawbacks.

The measurements themselves are challenging, such that only about 10 research laboratories in the world are routinely doing them. Calibrating the measurements is an ongoing challenge. Earth is not helping: Warmer waters hold less gas, meaning that as oceans warm in response to climate change, they expel some oxygen into the atmosphere. We must account for this in our carbon sink calculations. And to take into account variability in ocean circulation and other ocean processes, we have to average our results over 10-year time frames.

Policymakers and the public need answers faster. We believe the solution involves both improving the atmospheric oxygen approach and using other independent approaches: measurements of carbon and oxygen in the oceans, computer models and satellites are all essential. Combining these approaches will lead to more robust understanding of the carbon cycle and climate change, and better knowledge of where these valuable carbon sinks and the global climate are headed.

articles.title: To get Americans to care about climate change, just call it climate change
articles.author: Wändi Bruine de Bruin, Director of Behavioral Science & Policy Initiative, Schaeffer Institute of Public Policy & Government Service, USC Price School of Public Policy, USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences
paras: You may be hearing phrases like “climate crisis,” “climate emergency” and “climate justice” a lot as the 2026 United Nations climate summit is underway. Political leaders, including U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, are using them to try to get across the urgent risks and consequences of climate change. The danger is real, but is using this language actually persuasive?

It turns out that Americans are more familiar with – and more concerned about – climate change and global warming than they are about climate crisis, climate emergency or climate justice, according to a survey we conducted with a nationally representative sample of 5,137 Americans.
Moreover, we found no evidence that the alternative terms increased people’s sense of urgency, willingness to support climate-friendly policies or willingness to act.

The familiar terms – climate change and global warming – did at least as well, and sometimes better, than climate crisis and climate emergency in eliciting concern, perceived urgency and willingness to act. The phrase climate justice consistently tended to do worse, likely in part because it was the least familiar. These response patterns were similar among Republicans, Democrats and independents.
In our work as research psychologists, we have explored how Americans respond to the ways climate change is communicated and have uncovered a need to use straightforward language.

For example, people we interviewed for a study published in 2021 felt that climate experts were talking over their heads with terms like “adaptation,” “mitigation,” “sustainability” and “carbon-dioxide removal.” They wanted experts to use more familiar terms instead.

This inspired us to write a quick guide to climate jargon, published in The Conversation. Using everyday language makes information easier to understand, and even highly educated people tend to prefer it.

Jargon like “biodiversity loss” has similar problems. That refers to the shrinking variety of life on Earth, which is exacerbated by climate change. A survey of 7,338 U.S. adults led by one of us found people were much more familiar with and more concerned about “extinction of plants and animals” – or, if an explanation was provided, “nature loss”.

Even with an explanation, “biodiversity loss” was the least familiar and of least concern for people among several terms. Most people didn’t find “biodiversity crisis” or “extinction crisis” familiar either.
Yet, experts often use complex jargon because it is familiar to them, and they may not realize it is unfamiliar to others.

It has become common to talk about climate change and global warming as if they have the same meaning, but there are differences. Climate change refers to changes in the overall climate, while global warming refers specifically to rising temperatures.

A historical review found that, in the past, people were less likely to associate the term climate change with the idea that humans are actively warming the planet than they were with the term global warming. Perhaps this is why Democrats used to like the term global warming, while the popularization of the term climate change has been credited to Frank Luntz, an adviser to the George W. Bush administration.

Past surveys also found that Democrats used to think of global warming as being more serious than climate change, while Republicans thought of climate change as more serious than global warming. But according to a recent review, these partisan differences have now faded.

Alternative terms such as climate crisis, climate emergency and climate justice have been used to emphasize other aspects of climate change and to try to raise concern. In 2019, the British newspaper The Guardian switched to using climate crisis and climate emergency because it wanted to convey urgency.

Activists use the term climate justice to draw attention to climate change as a human rights challenge: Low-income people around the world suffer the most from the effects of climate change, despite being the least responsible for causing it.
The takeaway: Avoid overheated language
Right now, the terms climate crisis, climate emergency or climate justice are less familiar and elicit less concern than climate change or global warming.

Even if these terms become more commonplace, there is no guarantee that they will heighten concern or inspire action. In fact, studies have suggested that phrases like climate crisis could backfire if they don’t resonate with people.

Our advice: Don’t make the mistake of using overheated language. Just stick with familiar terms that people understand – use global warming when referring to rising temperatures and climate change for overall changes in the climate.
This updates an article originally published Aug. 12, 2024, with a new study and discussions at the 2026 U.N. climate conference, COP31.

articles.title: In a world of anti-environment backlash, Andy Burnham walks a line between popular and green
articles.author: Renaud Foucart, Senior Lecturer in Economics, Lancaster University Management School, Lancaster University
paras: Andy Burnham took to the floor at the UN climate summit, Cop31, in Turkey and promised a “new era of British leadership”.

The UK’s new prime minister does not talk a lot about the environment, and many of his recent decisions have disappointed environmental activists. Since late October, he has approved a new gas field in the North Sea. He decided to extend the freeze on fuel duty, and has floated reducing the electric vehicle target.

His government also recently reduced support for heat pumps. And his chancellor, John Healey, has recently said the government backs Heathrow airport’s project to build a third runway. Although some sources are reporting that Burnham has still not confirmed it.
Yet Burnham might end up being the saviour of Britain’s ambitious net zero agenda, the initiative to push countries to remove as much greenhouse gas as they emit by 2050.

His plan has a razor-sharp focus on consumers, and a by-product of this might be to cut fossil fuel use too. But along the way, he looks like he is ready to drop any decision that could make the broader agenda unpopular.

Just six months ago, the country looked like it might be on track for a Nigel Farage-led Reform right-wing populist government. Reform was well ahead of Labour and the Conservatives in the polls. And Farage does not hide his intention to scrap net zero targets if he ever gets into power.
Today, Labour is pulling further ahead in the polls. It would be useful to take seriously how Andy Burnham got there.
There are broadly three ways to promote environmental policy. One is de-growth: the idea that we can only save the planet by doing less.

Another is boosterism, the spirit behind Boris Johnson’s net zero idea. It promises a green revolution that unleashes decades of growth from new technologies. This works as a vision, but there can be a backlash when people face the short-term costs.
Then there is Andy Burnham’s: the consumer-first environmental agenda.
Why it might boost electricity use

Take the current electric vehicle target, that 80% of new cars sold in the UK must be electric by 2030. It looks like Burnham is happy to lower it if it can protect consumers from higher costs. But, so far, Britain has also chosen not to tax cheap Chinese car imports, unlike the European Union and the United States.
But around a third of Chinese imports are electric vehicles. So, this could push up EV use significantly.

The approval of the Jackdaw gas field, 150 miles off the Scottish coast, follows the same ruthless logic. Extracting gas domestically is not unambiguously bad for the environment. One argument is that if Britain does not exploit that field, it may end up importing even more polluting foreign gas instead. Although the benefits could be minimal.

Gas is traded globally, so Jackdaw will not affect global prices. But it will raise money for the government’s energy wealth fund. This will be spent on renewable investment and lower electricity bills.

Sometimes, supporting consumers also supports the environment. Cutting value added tax and green charges on electricity bills could encourage people to switch from gas boilers and petrol cars to heat pumps and electric vehicles.

This benefits the planet but also should make electricity cheaper for everyone down the line. A big driver of high electricity costs in Britain is the lack of demand: the cost of infrastructure is shared among too few consumers.

But, sometimes, supporting consumers means making decisions that totally conflict with the general goal. Take the decision to freeze fuel duty, which has appeared in every budget since 2011. Protecting consumers from higher petrol prices discourages people from switching to electric vehicles. That makes electricity more expensive for everyone. And it has cost the Treasury £139 billion so far.

However, motorists are way too dangerous to anger. Emmanuel Macron spent his two terms in France under the permanent threat of the yellow vest riots. The movement started with a complaint about petrol prices and speed limits.
So Burnham chooses not to anger them.

Then there’s the proposed plan to build a third runway at Heathrow. Burnham, a champion of decentralisation, has never been a fan of the London-centred project. But it appears that he may (or may not) now back it. Certainly his chancellor thinks so.
To understand why, it can be useful to look at the project impact assessment. Expanding Heathrow would potentially be bad for the environment and good for the economy.
The project is expected to bring passengers more than £20 billion in direct economic benefits, and cheaper airfares.

Current congestion at Heathrow means airlines can charge very high prices, for instance during school holidays. So a third runway could open up competition, and bring fares down. So it looks like Burnham may be willing to cut part of his environmental goals to let Britons afford some cheaper trips abroad.
But, overall, it is unclear how much of his broader political agenda Burnham must sacrifice for social acceptability. He must also try and balance this with encouraging investment in Britain.

With anti-environmental populism on the rise around the world, Burnham’s current popularity is based on getting this balance right. If he can, it might be a sign he could quietly deliver a new era of British leadership, and a stealthy boost for the environment.

articles.title: Could you survive without Microsoft? Inside the costs of digital dependence
articles.author: Narmin Nahidi, Assistant Professor in Finance, University of Exeter
paras: When I arrived at work to discover that Outlook had vanished from my computer, I wondered how I was supposed to get through my working day. No emails. No calendar. No meeting invitations.

Then another thought crossed my mind: when did we become so dependent on a single technology company that losing access to one application could disrupt our entire working routine? And what is the financial and environmental cost of that dependence?

We regularly discuss sustainability in terms of reducing plastic, cutting carbon emissions and consuming less energy. But the digital systems we rely on every day also have huge environmental consequences.

As world leaders gather at the UN climate summit, Cop31, in Turkey, perhaps it is time to ask an uncomfortable question: can our digital economy really become sustainable when so much of it depends on a handful of technology companies?
The cloud has a physical footprint
The cloud may sound weightless, but it runs on data centres, electricity, cooling systems and hardware.

The International Energy Agency estimates that data centres consumed 415 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024, around 1.5% of global demand. It projects that consumption could reach 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, largely driven by AI and other digital services.

Microsoft’s own 2026 sustainability report illustrates the tension. The company reported a 25% year-over-year rise in total emissions in 2025, primarily because of expanding data centres and a change in renewable-energy certificate accounting. Microsoft is also investing in cleaner energy and more efficient infrastructure. Both facts matter: technological progress can reduce emissions per task, while growth pushes overall demand higher.
Asking the right questions

Turkey’s Cop31 presidency released the voluntary Antalya artificial intelligence pledge in October. This pledge aims to encourage climate-responsible AI while acknowledging the energy and water demands of the technology.

The World Resources Institute, a global research organisation, welcomed the pledge’s direction but warned that voluntary commitments need stronger accountability mechanisms. Meanwhile, the International Telecommunication Union has scheduled a Cop31 event for November 16 on financing cleaner digital infrastructure, measuring emissions, and promoting durable, repairable and reusable electronics.

The message is important: sustainability cannot stop at greener electricity. It also concerns what technology organisations purchase, how long they keep it, and who pays for its environmental effects.
When a software decision becomes a hardware bill

Consider a computer that still works but cannot support a newer operating system. Windows 10’s regular support ended in October 2025, although Microsoft offers extended security updates for eligible consumer devices through October 2027.
The transition does not make every older computer obsolete. Yet software support and compatibility can influence whether organisations replace otherwise usable equipment.

Manufacturing devices consumes energy and raw materials. It also creates electronic waste (e-waste). According to the UN’s global e-waste monitor, the world generated 62 million metric tonnes of e-waste in 2022, of which just 22.3% was documented as formally collected and recycled.
These figures cover all electronic waste, not waste attributable to Microsoft. They nevertheless show why extending equipment lifetimes deserves a place in climate policy.
Costs that are rarely counted
A software subscription has a visible price. Less visible are the costs of training employees, migrating files, replacing equipment, maintaining duplicate systems and eventually switching suppliers.
Economists call these switching costs. They can lock organisations into existing providers even when better-value alternatives emerge.

This is not merely hypothetical. In March 2026, the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority announced plans to investigate Microsoft’s business software ecosystem. It also reported steps by major cloud service providers, including Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services, to reduce data-transfer fees and improve interoperability, making it easier for businesses to switch between providers.

What might this have to do with sustainability? A buyer unable to change providers easily may also struggle to choose lower-emission computing services. That is a potential environmental consequence of lock-in, not a demonstrated claim that Microsoft users emit more carbon.

There is a wider accounting problem too. The UN estimates that global electronic waste was associated with approximately US$78 billion (£59 billion) in externalised costs in 2022, including pollution and climate-related impacts. Such costs are largely absent from the price of a software license.
A responsible procurement decision should therefore compare lifetime financial costs, equipment lifespans and credible emissions data rather than only the next annual bill.
Could workplaces use alternatives (such as Thunderbird and LibreOffice) or interoperable cloud services? Often, yes. But migration has costs and a rival provider is not necessarily greener.
The better goal is freedom to choose: portable data, open document formats, repairable devices, transparent environmental reporting and software contracts that do not penalise switching.
Digital systems that remain affordable, competitive and environmentally responsible, even when their preferred technology changes, will be the most resilient ones.

articles.title: Young turtles find refuge in both natural and artificial wetlands in UAE – new study
articles.author: Owen Exeter, Postdoctoral Researcher, Marine Ecology, University of Exeter
paras: Coastal wetlands, such as mangroves and saltmarshes, are rapidly disappearing yet they are incredibly important for young turtles.

In a new study, my colleagues and I used satellite tags to track young green turtles in a protected wetland in Sharjah, UAE. Our results reveal just how important these remaining natural spaces are to young turtles.

But we also found that nature can find a way to thrive in unexpected, human-made environments too. So protecting these habitats and the connections between wetlands, artificial environments and the open sea is essential to ensuring wildlife can persist in an increasingly human-shaped world.

Coastal wetlands protect our shorelines from storms, store carbon and provide important nursery habitats for marine life. Yet scientists still know surprisingly little about how marine wildlife, including turtles, sharks and rays, use these environments. Knowing where these animals feed, shelter and move helps identify which areas need protection and whether existing protected areas are working.

Our study, a collaborative effort between the Environment and Protected Areas Authority (EPAA), a UAE government agency, the University of Exeter and the Sharjah Marine Science Research Centre, focused on Al Qurm Wa Lehhfaiiah, a marine protected area encompassing the last major coastal wetland ecosystem on the UAE’s east coast, which is called Khor Kalba.

Its complex wetlands support migratory wading birds, numerous fish species and the Arabian collared kingfisher, a subspecies found only in this region. Young green turtles also swim through its winding mangrove channels.

Although the wetland is now protected and recognised as a Ramsar site, a type of conservation designation for any internationally important wetlands, it has not escaped human development. The city of Kalba surrounds much of the site, and a large human-made basin (like a lagoon) was built alongside the natural mangroves in the early 2000s as a proposed recreational and commercial waterfront. The basin was never used for its intended recreational purposes and has since been incorporated into the protected area.

To understand how young turtles use this unusual landscape alongside the natural mangrove channels, EPAA staff carefully captured nine juvenile green turtles in 2019 and attached satellite tags to their shells using a specialist, harmless resin. After the turtles were released, the tags allowed us to follow their movements.

After seven months and over 2,800 satellite locations the results were clear. We found Kalba’s wetlands were a critical habitat for all nine turtles. They generally stayed within just 2 miles of the wetland entrance and spent more than 80% of their tracked time inside the marine protected area’s boundary.

One of the more surprising findings was the popularity of the human-made basin (similar to a saltwater lagoon extending from the mangroves). The turtles were around five times more likely to be found there than elsewhere in the wetland, and 77% of their core-use areas were concentrated within it.

We cannot say for certain why the turtles favoured the basin. One possibility is that algae growing on its floor provides food, while its enclosed layout may offer shelter from larger predators. Whatever the explanation, the findings suggest that wildlife can make use of human-modified environments.

However, this is no substitute for protecting natural habitats. Where coastal environments are modified or restored, designs that retain natural habitats, maintain connections between them and preserve the ecological processes they depend on may offer the greatest benefits for wildlife.

One turtle eventually embarked on a very different journey. After remaining in the wetland for 93 days, it travelled over 500 miles to Masirah Island in neighbouring Oman. This remarkable journey highlights how a small coastal wetland can be important to young turtles before they move into wider waters.

But the study also revealed a gap in protection. The main natural channel connecting the ocean to the mangroves and basin currently lies outside the marine protected area. Although the turtles used this channel less frequently overall, they gathered there at low tide, possibly waiting for rising water to allow them to move back into the wetland. Extending protection to include this connecting channel could therefore strengthen the conservation value of the entire system.

Our findings underline the importance of protecting natural coastal wetlands. The human-made basin may offer unexpected benefits, but the natural mangrove channels and their connection to the sea remain essential parts of the wider ecosystem.

As coastal development continues around the world, understanding how wildlife uses both natural and modified environments can help us make better conservation decisions. Protecting the remaining wetlands at Kalba, including the connections between them and the ocean, is an important step towards securing a future for the young turtles that depend on them.

articles.title: Far from farms and cities, dry climates are boosting river nitrate pollution
articles.author: Li Li (李黎), Professor of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Penn State
paras: Typically, when people hear about nitrates, it involves runoff from farm fields, sewage systems and cities that can fuel harmful algae blooms and raise the risk of a serious illness in infants known as “blue baby syndrome.”

But a river can also run through a sparsely populated landscape with little farming and still contain surprisingly high levels of this form of nitrogen that can harm aquatic life, drinking water and human health.

In a new study, my colleague and I found a reason why that happens: Dry climate conditions are associated with high river nitrate concentrations, even in places with little farming or urban development.

We found nitrate hot spots in some unexpected places, including the Rocky Mountains of the western United States and northern Africa’s Sahara Desert. Where water is scarce, we found that nitrates – which can naturally leach into surface water and groundwater from the soil as microbes break down organic material – were able to accumulate and become concentrated rather than being diluted or flushed away.

That raises health concerns for regions where nitrates in rivers and well water might not be given much thought. It also raises questions about how nitrate-related health risks will increase as global temperatures rise.

To see how widespread this pattern is, we combined global measurements from more than 7,000 monitoring sites and additionally extracted information about climate, soils, land use and other landscape features. We then trained machine learning models to estimate long-term average nitrate concentrations across nearly 2.9 million river segments worldwide.
The resulting map suggests that nitrates deserve attention well beyond the urban and agricultural regions where they are usually monitored.

High nitrate exposure in water and food is particularly dangerous for infants because it can interfere with the blood’s ability to carry oxygen. Blue baby syndrome, or methemoglobinemia, can result in serious illnesses and be caused by nitrate poisoning.
The U.S. drinking water standard of 10 milligrams of nitrate-nitrogen per liter was established primarily to guard against this acute risk.
We estimate that about 37,000 people worldwide live in areas where rivers exceed the 10 mg/L drinking water standard, predominantly in the U.S. Corn Belt.

That doesn’t mean 37,000 people are drinking water at those concentrations, since river water in many regions is treated before it is supplied for drinking. But it’s a concerning level they should be aware of, particularly those using well water.

Research has also raised concerns about possible effects of long-term exposure to nitrate at lower concentrations, including certain cancers and adverse birth outcomes, such as babies born preterm or with a low birth weight, although those risks are still being studied.
We estimate that about 480 million people worldwide live in areas where nearby rivers have elevated long-term average nitrate concentrations, above 2.5 milligrams per liter.

Many of the rivers our models identified as having elevated nitrate levels are small headwater streams. Many headwater streams cease to flow for some periods of time every year, and nitrates can accumulate to high concentrations under dry or low-flow conditions. These small streams make up most of the global river networks, have long been overlooked and feed larger rivers that supply drinking water to large populations and help shape the quality of water downstream.
Too much nitrate in rivers and lakes can also fuel algal growth and disrupt aquatic ecosystems.

A global map of nitrate concentrations in river water cannot show what comes out of someone’s tap. Their water may be mixed with other sources or treated before they drink it. Nitrate concentrations can also rise and fall over time, while our map shows long-term averages.
To understand a person’s actual exposure will require connecting river measurements with drinking water sources, treatment practices and tests of water delivered to households.

Many rivers with nitrate concentrations above 2.5 milligrams per liter flow through sparsely populated regions where access to treated drinking water may be limited. Even where treatment facilities exist, conventional methods remove little nitrate. Removing it requires specialized technologies that can be costly to operate.

Our study shows why more drylands and small headwater streams need to be monitored for nitrate. It also raises a question for a warming world: If a region becomes drier, how much will nitrate concentrations rise even if people do not add more nitrogen to the landscape?

Answering that will require measurements through wet and dry periods, paired with studies of how water moves through soils, groundwater and rivers. For now, the message is clear: Protecting water quality requires paying attention to the climate as well as to the human activities that put nitrogen into the environment.

articles.title: Extreme weather risk is scaring big corporations away from poorer countries – that hurts the companies, too
articles.author: Jonas Gamso, Associate Professor of International Trade and Global Studies, Arizona State University
paras: When multinational companies decide where to build a factory, open a mine or establish a regional office, they have to consider whether the investment will still be profitable years into the future.

Making that decision increasingly means thinking about risks, like whether surrounding roads will flood, worker safety will be compromised by extreme heat in the summer, and clean water will be available.

As climate change increases the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events around the world, these effects can be especially severe in poorer countries that lack the resources to prepare for disasters or recover quickly after they hit.

I study how political and environmental risks affect international business. In my new book, “Multinational Corporations and Climate Change: Risks, Responsibilities, and Resilience,” I explore how disaster risk is affecting the ways global companies see these climate-vulnerable markets, and how those views are leading some foreign investors to avoid these developing nations altogether.

Low- and middle-income countries aren’t the only ones that suffer when multinational corporations pass them by. The companies themselves also stand to lose out on business opportunities in emerging markets if they pull away.
How climate risk affects foreign investment

Evidence from several studies suggests that multinationals are systematically avoiding investing in the most climate-vulnerable countries. These include my own analysis of 159 countries. Although these studies focus on different samples, they identify the same trend: Countries characterized by greater climate vulnerability received less foreign investment.

The results are not trivial. My book identifies a 12% reduction in foreign direct investment for each 1-point rise in climate vulnerability on a 100-point scale, while holding other relevant factors constant. This vulnerability data measures countries’ exposure to climate hazards as well as their capacity to adapt.
Companies rarely say why they’re avoiding a particular location, but their climate-related concerns occasionally become visible.

For example, Google halted plans to build a US$200 million data center in Chile after an environmental court revoked its construction permit over the likely effects on water supplies and the environment. Similarly, a $1 billion data center proposed in Kenya by Microsoft and the Abu Dhabi-based artificial intelligence company G42 was delayed and ultimately suspended amid concerns about water stress in the area.
Companies have reason to be cautious about climate risks.

One analysis of 71 large publicly traded companies found that firms reporting major flood losses experienced a 5% average decline in shareholder value over the following year, after accounting for broader market movements.
In Vietnam, typhoons and floods caused an estimated $475 million in damage to energy and transportation infrastructure in 2022. Unreliable infrastructure cost companies there about $280 million.

Severe flooding in Thailand in 2011 forced several companies, including Toyota, Nissan and Honda, to temporarily suspend production as factories flooded, shutting down production of parts or vehicles made there.
Costs like those shape where companies choose to invest next.

While climate risk does not stop all investment in climate-vulnerable markets, it does make projects in these nations relatively more expensive, less attractive and more difficult to finance than less risky locations.
Who loses from investor avoidance?

For developing countries, less foreign investment means fewer jobs are created. These countries also have fewer opportunities to benefit from exposure to the new technologies that multinationals bring when they invest abroad.

Those results highlight another way climate change is deepening global inequality. It reduces the economic activity that could support future development, while simultaneously damaging physical infrastructure and threatening human health and well-being.

Developing countries are especially vulnerable to the effects of rising global temperatures, whether for their dependence on agricultural markets, geography or relatively fragile infrastructure. A report from the Climate Impact Lab at the University of Chicago projects that 90% of heat-related deaths in the coming decades will take place in low- and middle-income countries. Similarly, a 2022 study found that around 90% of people exposed to flooding live in developing nations.

Yet poor countries have contributed only a tiny fraction of the emissions that are causing climate change, even as they face the brunt of the damage. For example, African countries are responsible for less than 4% of greenhouse gas emissions globally. But they stand to experience the greatest negative effects of climate change.
Lost opportunities for multinational companies
When a company avoids investing in climate-vulnerable countries, that may reduce its exposure to floods, droughts or extreme heat, but the decision also carries potential costs for the company.

Many of these countries have growing consumer markets, energy resources or critical minerals that multinationals need. Companies that dismiss them as too risky may lose out on promising opportunities.

For example, the Democratic Republic of Congo supplies most of the world’s cobalt, while Indonesia has become the dominant producer of nickel. These countries are highly vulnerable to climate change, which is likely scaring some companies away.

Yet companies with a greater tolerance for risk have established strong positions in those countries’ mineral industries. Thus, more cautious firms may reduce their risk exposure, but they are also surrendering access to important resources and growing markets.
Reducing investor avoidance
There are ways to help companies overcome their climate-risk avoidance so more investment can pour into these countries:

Foreign aid from wealthy countries can help developing countries shore up their roads, ports, electrical grids and water systems before extreme storms or droughts occur. My 2025 study found that climate-vulnerable countries that received more aid for climate adaptation also received more foreign direct investment than those receiving less aid. The result suggests the funding may reassure companies that climate risks are being addressed.

International development banks can share some of the risks by providing climate risk insurance to multinationals. This would offer a safety net to absorb some of the losses if a covered disruption prevents a project from operating as intended. The World Bank already offers similar coverage against political risk incidents, which has given companies confidence to invest in countries such as Kenya, Mozambique and Nigeria.

Better data can give companies more precise information about climate risks. Many risk scores label entire nations as vulnerable or not, even though exposure varies from one city or project site to another. More detailed information about local flood exposure, water availability, heat, infrastructure and adaptation capabilities would allow companies to limit their avoidance to the riskiest areas, instead of bypassing those countries altogether.

Understanding the local risk, insuring companies against risk and helping countries make their infrastructure more resilient to storms, droughts and heat can help boost investment in ways that benefit the companies and spur economic growth and development in climate-vulnerable countries at the same time.

articles.title: El Niño threatens health, too – early warnings done right can save lives
articles.author: Kimberley Miner, Research Professor in Earth Sciences, University of Maine
paras: As communities around the world shore up their infrastructure in anticipation of one of the most powerful El Niños on record in late 2026 and early 2027, they need to think about rising health risks, too – and include them in early weather warnings.

El Niño is part of a natural climate phenomenon that shifts global weather patterns for months at a time. During El Niño years, global temperatures tend to rise, triggering heat waves; normally dry regions can be hit with flooding rainfall; and normally wet regions often face droughts. All carry serious health risks.

In southern Africa, for example, forecasters are warning of a rising risk of severe drought that could affect the 2026-27 growing season in key farming regions. At the same time, wetter-than-normal conditions in the Horn of Africa raise the risk of flooding and mosquito-borne disease outbreaks there.

Dry conditions in Southeast Asia are already fueling wildfires and sending water supplies falling. October downpours in Chile triggered mudslides that left a mess for people to clean up in homes and yards.
In the United States, the South tends to be wetter than normal during El Niño years; drought is more likely in the Northern Plains; and storms can be fierce, particularly along the Pacific Coast.
As researchers in psychology, global health and Earth system science, we study how environmental disruptions affect people’s health and their ability to respond.
To protect the population, communities need plans that keep care accessible and weather warnings that provide advice people can act on before, during and after a disaster.
When extreme weather becomes a health emergency
The health consequences of extreme weather events often extend beyond the immediate hazard.
For example, research has linked exposure to flooding, wildfire and ecosystem changes with elevated risks of illnesses, psychological distress and chronic stress.

Floodwater can lead to infections, such as hepatitis, cryptosporidium and fungal diseases, as well as longer-term health damage through exposure to harmful environmental microbes, chemicals and an increase in disease-carrying vectors such as mosquitoes.
Drought can lead to poor air quality and, in some places, malnutrition.
Disasters can also keep people from getting essential healthcare, disrupt their livelihoods and displace them from their homes and social networks.

The threat of a changing, potentially unsafe environment can also increase anticipatory, long-term distress. The World Health Organization identifies anxiety and post-traumatic stress as mental health consequences of extreme weather-related hazards. We believe mental health counseling services also belong in communities’ preparedness and recovery plans, not as an optional add-on after addressing physical needs.
Vulnerable populations face even higher risks

For people with existing illnesses or in areas far from medical care, extreme weather brings additional risks. These individuals and healthcare systems benefit from early warnings about El Niño’s disaster risks that help them prepare well in advance.

At least 2.5 million Americans rely on in-home electricity-powered medical equipment, such as oxygen concentrators and ventilators, including nearly 78,000 who receive dialysis at home to help their kidneys function. When the power goes out or water is disrupted, they risk losing use of what may be life-sustaining equipment.

Distance compounds these risks. Many communities around the world don’t have local clinics. Rural Americans live an average of 10.5 miles (17 kilometers) from the nearest hospital, and for 1 in 4 rural residents, the trip takes more than 30 minutes on average – before a single road floods. During Hurricane Harvey in 2017, flooding limited access to Houston’s second-busiest hospital for five days. The most extensive disruptions were in lower-income and minority neighborhoods.

With advanced warnings, community organizations and healthcare providers preparing for El Niño can contact people with health vulnerabilities early to arrange backup power supplies and help them prepare so they know what to do when disasters do strike.
How to turn forecasts into protection
A good weather warning doesn’t just name the threat. It also provides information that residents can act on to stay safe through the disaster and the recovery afterward.

Communities do not need to wait until a disaster is building to begin preparing. Existing community emergency plans, patient outreach programs and social networks provide a starting point for steps that help.
First, communities can identify where disruptions could become public health emergencies.

State departments of health and other social services can combine regional weather outlooks with local information about areas facing the highest risks, including the health impacts of water exposure on homes, guidance for avoiding polluted floodwaters and evacuation routes.
Community organizations can help identify individuals and neighborhoods that may face language barriers and ensure they receive lifesaving alerts and information they can understand.
Second, it’s important to protect continuity of clinical care for patients during disasters.

Health systems and public health departments can coordinate with health providers in hospitals, pharmacies and home health services to identify people who depend on regular medical appointments or transportation and ensure they can still receive care.
In practice, this may be providing flexible scheduling options, organizing alternative means of transportation or identifying alternative care locations that may be more accessible.
Third, weather warnings can be most useful when they provide information people can act on, such as where to find food, transportation or mental health support.

Many local and state emergency services already work to educate the public about storm risks ahead. They can do more by also telling residents where they can find safe water and food, how to limit exposure to chemicals or disease vectors, how to store medicine safely, and whom to contact for transportation, shelter or mental health support.
Information that is specific enough to use and relevant to the community can save lives.
Preparation is preventive care

Because signs of the coming weather shift can be detected months in advance, El Niño forecasts offer something that immediate storm forecasts can’t: extra time to identify these health risks, secure medical care for the months ahead and prepare so warnings are useful to residents.
When warnings pair information about the risk with practical actions and local resources, they can empower people rather than leaving them feeling helpless in the face of a disaster.

articles.title: The SS United States has been deliberately sunk – this is how marine life will colonise the world’s largest artificial reef
articles.author: Nicholas Ray, Doctoral Programmes Manager and Researcher in Aquatic Ecology, Nottingham Trent University
paras: As a marine ecologist and keen scuba diver, I’ve long been fascinated by what happens when a large structure is introduced to the sea. Within hours, microscopic organisms begin colonising its surfaces, forming a thin biological layer. Over the following months and years, barnacles, mussels, sponges and other marine life become established, creating a new habitat that attracts fish and a diverse range of species.

This week, one of the world’s most famous ocean liners, the SS United States, was sunk off the coast of Florida. At 302 metres long, it has become the world’s largest artificial reef. It is a very exciting prospect to one day dive on such a giant, and to see how it changes as marine life makes it home.

The SS United States was built as a luxury ocean liner, and its maiden voyage in 1952 captured the coveted Blue Riband by crossing the Atlantic in only three days and ten hours – a passenger liner record that remains unbroken.

As the years went by, commercial jetliners superseded transatlantic sea travel, and the vessel was retired and neglected for decades. Rather than facing the ignominy of a breaker’s yard, the legendary ship was bought by Okaloosa County, Florida, to turn it into a diving attraction.

The SS United States is a particularly enormous structure to introduce to the seabed – longer even than the Titanic. It will rest in around 55 metres of water, with its upper sections rising to within about 17 metres of the surface. This will create habitats at different depths, making it an unusually varied site for both wildlife and divers of different abilities.
It will also eclipse the nearby 275-metre aircraft carrier USS Oriskany, deliberately sunk in 2006, to become the largest artificial reef on Earth.
So what do we expect to happen? Here’s a suggested ecological succession pattern, month-by-month.
First, microorganisms arrive

The first organisms to colonise the SS United States will be almost invisible. Within hours of immersion, marine bacteria and microalgae will begin attaching themselves to its cleaned metal surfaces, forming a thin layer of “biofilm”.

This slime is the foundation of the new ecosystem. As the biofilm develops, it releases chemical cues that help drifting larvae recognise the surface as a suitable place to settle. Carried by Gulf currents, these tiny organisms begin attaching themselves to the structure. By the end of the first three months, a variety of small animals and algae will have established themselves on the hull, beginning the transformation of bare metal into a living reef.
Then the ship becomes covered in marine life

As the biofilm matures, larger organisms arrive to feed on it. These include more mobile invertebrates like sea urchins and porcelain crabs, and filter-feeders like oysters and mussels which attach themselves to vertical walls where the currents tend to send the most nutrients their way.
Fish and larger predators move in

By the end of the first year, hard corals will begin to establish themselves permanently. The transformation will still be in its early stages, but over the next five to ten years the hull will become increasingly encrusted with corals, sponges and other marine life. At some point, casual divers will no longer see a ship covered in coral, but a coral-covered reef that happens to contain a ship.
As the reef develops, fish will be attracted by the shelter and the growing supply of food. Smaller fish will begin to find refuge to evade open-water predators.

Snappers and groupers are among the medium-sized reef fish that will begin to take up permanent residency around the wreck, using the long internal corridors for protection. Larger predators, including barracuda, king mackerel and sharks, could also patrol its decks and upper sections.

The ship’s enormous size and varied structure will offer a range of habitats, from sheltered spaces for smaller fish to exposed areas where larger, free-swimming species can hunt. Over time, these interactions could create a complex food web, turning the wreck into a significant biological hotspot.

A common misconception is that artificial reefs simply concentrate fish that were already present, leaving surrounding waters poorer. In reality, while some fish are attracted from elsewhere, a large reef structure also creates vast amounts of new habitat and food.

As corals, sponges, barnacles and other reef builders colonise the wreck, they create food and shelter that did not previously exist, allowing the ecosystem to support more life overall. The result is generally not an underwater crowd gathered around a ship, but a gradual increase in the total amount of marine life the area can support.

Another widespread misconception is that marine scientists “seed” artificial reefs with organisms or their larvae. In reality, colonisation happens naturally: the Gulf of Mexico already harbours an abundant pool of drifting larvae and migratory fish. Artificially introducing marine life is unnecessary and risks introducing non-native species or pathogens.

Instead, human engineering is largely about preparing the ship for sinking. This includes removing hazards such as oil, asbestos and loose wires, and sealing off parts of the vessel to prevent divers getting disorientated or lost in silt-outs deep in the hull.

The scuttling of the SS United States represents a rare convergence of maritime history, ecology, and engineering. Transformed into the world’s largest artificial reef, this record-breaking ocean liner could potentially anchor a vibrant marine ecosystem for decades to come. I’m looking forward to seeing how that transformation unfolds – and maybe, one day, exploring it myself.

articles.title: UK appoints new climate security envoy – here’s what she could change
articles.author: James Dyke, Assistant Director of the Global Systems Institute, University of Exeter
paras: The UK government has just appointed Madeleine Alessandri as the world’s first special representative for climate security.

Prime minister Andy Burnham announced the new role in his speech at the UN climate summit, Cop31, in Turkey. This, he said, would be part of “a new era of British leadership on climate”. He also cited climate as “a national security issue” – a sign that Burnham considers this environmental crisis a significant risk to the country’s social stability and economy.
With a remit to “support ministers to champion UK leadership on climate and nature security”, Alessandri will report to the foreign secretary.

Climate change has long been considered as a threat multiplier because it compounds and increases many risks to national security. Unfortunately, many governments have failed to acknowledge such threats, resulting in a dangerous blind spot.

For example, a warmer world will produce more erratic weather that will impact harvests. Less food produces price spikes. In order to try to ensure food security, governments implement export controls. This can cause globally traded food prices to spike driving people into food poverty, exacerbate tensions and lead to conflict.
The 2026 UK harvest is the worst on record. Four of the five worst harvests have happened since 2020. This puts further pressure on UK farmers.

As climate security envoy, one of Alessandri’s priorities will need to be the state of national food security. That’s because the UK imports 40% of the food it consumes and so is extremely exposed to the tightening of global food supply.

Given that this year’s super El Niño (when certain parts of the Pacific are warmer than usual) is already creating havoc around the world, Alessandri may soon find herself embroiled in efforts to ensure that the responses to the consequences of the climate crisis do not make the situation worse.

Responding to extreme weather and climate consequences can produce derailment risks whereby efforts to reduce climate change get blown off course by escalating climate and social destabilisation. For example, in response to rising food insecurity national governments can ban food exports. This increases food prices even further. Protests over the cost of living can spiral into wider unrest. All this can make it difficult to maintain the political will required to progress the energy transition.

Alessandri is a career civil servant and the former chair of the UK’s joint intelligence committee (JIC) which oversees the UK’s secret intelligence services. Until now, the security implications of climate change sat within Katie White’s remit as the UK’s minister for climate transition in the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero.

It is perhaps no coincidence that it was the JIC that commissioned the previously supressed report on the national security implications of climate change. While published by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, it is widely acknowledged that the national security assessment on global ecosystems was produced by the JIC while Allesandri was leading it.

She will now be in a position to negotiate directly with other nations and organisations specifically about the food and wider security impacts of climate change. I would expect other governments to create similar roles in the near future because climate change is rapidly rising up the ranks of issues that are relevant to national security.

articles.title: Climate change has different consequences for the health of women and men – but the systems tracking it don’t reflect that
articles.author: Kent Buse, Professor of Health Policy, Director of Programme Development, Monash University Malaysia, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, Monash University; Imperial College London
paras: The health risks men and women are exposed to and the illnesses they develop vary widely across lifetimes and places. Yet climate policy and health services often overlook these differences.

Some of these differences are stark. For example, more women than men die from being exposed to the smoke of cooking fires, but for most of adult life a man is more likely to die from this exposure than a woman of the same age. In Europe, studies of individual heatwaves have found women to be at higher risk of heat-related death.

In Latin America and the Caribbean though, men die from heat-related causes at nearly twice the rate that women do, according to the Global Burden of Disease study. Coordinated by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, this study is the largest systematic effort ever made to count what kills people and what makes them ill, producing comparable estimates of deaths, disease and disability for every country, by age and sex, every year since 1990.

Despite these inequities, the monitoring systems that track climate change and its effects on health fail to capture the full picture. Much of the data is categorised by gender when collected, but when the data is transferred to the monitoring systems, the experiences of women and men are merged into a single total. As a result, the decision-making that informs climate policy and health systems is underpinned by data that is oversimplified.

We have just audited four of those systems: the Belém Adaptation Indicators agreed at last year’s UN climate summit in Brazil, the World Health Organization’s survey of health ministries, a scorecard that grades countries’ climate plans on health and the Lancet Countdown, an annual scientific stock take. Of the 45 indicators from across these four reports that measure people’s lives (rather than tracking systems or plans), only one reports results separately for women and men.

All four reports draw on surveys and death registers that are often separated by sex, then published as one merged figure. That total is what reaches the people who decide what counts as progress and where the money goes.

That might be a philanthropic funder choosing which programmes to back, a government filling in the UN’s new adaptation scorecard in the only format its definitions allow, or the negotiators who will use those scorecards to judge whether the world is adapting in 2028 at Cop33.
At the UN climate summit Cop31, currently underway in Antalya, Turkey, we have an opportunity to change what gets reported in the future about how climate affects men and women’s health.

Sex and gender shape climate risk. Data is often reported by sex but then differences are explained by a combination of sex and gender (social roles, norms, structures). The biological makeup of human bodies affects how they physiologically respond differently to heat and smoke. Pregnancy brings additional risks.
The gendered norms of daily life put women and men in different places and situations: who works on a building site in 40°C heat, who cooks indoors over wood, who can get to a clinic.
It is easy to assume that women bear the greater risk. Often they do, but only accurately categorised data can tell us if that is always the case.

Women are more exposed to smoke from cooking stoves, for example, and it claims a larger share of their overall ill health, yet it kills more men. This is because men often reach midlife with hearts and lungs already damaged by a range of factors such as smoking and by the dust, fumes and diesel exhaust of working in mines, on building sites, farms and near traffic, so a smaller exposure to cooking smoke does greater damage.

The point is not to pit the sexes against each other. Knowing why they differ, whether through exposure, susceptibility or access to cooling, transport or care, tells you where to intervene. A single total hides all of that nuance.

We assessed a total of 211 indicators based on whether they reveal whether women and men are affected differently. Only the Lancet Countdown’s count of outdoor workers does. Of the 166 indicators that measure plans, systems and environments, only five mention sex or gender in some way.
A publishing decision, not a data gap

For much of this gap, the data already exists. The Lancet Countdown’s own methods appendix shows that three of its indicators use data split by sex and then merge it before publication. The Belém indicators that count people will draw on household surveys, death registers and workforce records, which routinely report by sex. These could be published by sex in the next reporting cycle with little or no new data collection.
Where the data is really missing or scattered, filling the gap costs money, and that is where climate and health funders could make the most difference.
The Belém indicators are the UN’s new yardstick for whether countries are adapting to climate change, but the details of each indicator remain to be written.

Decisions still need to be made at the global level on what each indicator measures, which data sources they use, and whether results are broken down by groups such as women and men. These detailed definitions, the output of a technical working group, are due to be agreed in November 2027.

Countries will then build their reporting systems around them. The record so far is not encouraging. Of the 16 expert proposals for health indicators circulated in May 2025, three asked for results by sex. By September 2025 there was one. The eight adopted at Cop30 in November 2025 include none.

The technical group was due to be formed in June 2026, but governments could not agree who should sit on it, so the decision returns to Cop31. If it includes people who know how to produce statistics by sex, and if reporting by sex becomes the default wherever the source data already have it, the next decade of climate adaptation can show who it reached – and who is being left behind.

We will repeat our audit as each framework updates. This means that governments will know whether their adaptation is reaching men and women equitably according to need. Funders will know whether their money is.
